items.summary: SlothPlan: the to-do list that does less My entry for the Hacktoberfest Week 3 "Slow and Steady" challenge — built for International Sloth Day, with open-weight models, zero API costs, and a philosophy I'd actually live by. The problem My to-do list has 47 items. Yours probably does too. And here's the dirty secret of productivity culture: the list isn't the work. Triaging the list is the work — the staring, the re-ordering, the guilt-math of "is learning Spanish more important than calling the dentist?" I have spent entire Sunday mornings reorganizing tasks instead of doing them, which is just procrastination wearing a planner's clothes. Every to-do app on the planet answers this with more features: priorities, tags, Eisenhower matrices, AI scheduling assistants that need your calendar, your email, your soul, and a $12/month subscription. They make the triage heavier . Nobody built the app that does the triage for you and then — this is the important part — tells you to do less. So for "Slow and Steady" I built exactly that: a tool that rewards laziness by doing the one piece of work you were avoiding (deciding what matters), capping your day at three things, and granting you written permission to delete the rest. What I built SlothPlan — a command-line tool where you dump a messy to-do list and get back three buckets: DO TODAY (max 3, non-negotiable), DEFER (officially not today's problem), and DELETE (permission granted, let it go). Each item gets a one-line reason. The judgment comes from a local open-weight model; the guarantees come from deterministic code. python3 -m slothplan triage -f my-messy-todos.txt The twist, same as my Week 2 entry: the model, the inference engine, and all the code run on your own machine. No account. No API key. No subscription. Your to-do list — which is, let's be honest, a map of your anxieties — never touches a network. The demo (real transcript, unedited) I fed it a 12-item Tuesday dump. Here is what the recorded run produced (full transcript in the repo's demo-output.txt — nothing cherry-picked): === SLOTHPLAN triage === method: rule-based fallback (--no-llm was passed; no model was run) DO TODAY (max 3) — your only decisions today: 1. Pay electricity bill, due Friday or they cut the power -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event 2. Reply to Priya about the wedding RSVP — deadline is tomorrow -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event 3. Submit the Hacktoberfest Week 3 entry README tonight -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event DEFER — officially not today's problem: 4. Call dentist to reschedule the appointment -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy] 12. Call mom back — she called twice today -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy] DELETE — permission granted, let it go: 10. Delete that crypto spam email from "DOUBLE YOUR COINS" -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost 11. Reorganize my Netflix watchlist -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost That's the deterministic mode ( --no-llm ), and it's the mode I'd actually use daily: three real obligations surfaced, the dentist and mom politely bounced by the cap with an explanation, and the crypto spam and the Netflix-watchlist reorganization sentenced to death. Twelve decisions I didn't have to make. Now the confession, because the transcript has two runs and I'm not hiding the first one: when I let the 0.5B model judge all 12 items itself, it took "rewards laziness" as a personal mission. It deleted the electricity bill . It called buying milk "spam". It deleted calling my mother. Every verdict parsed cleanly — 12/12, zero fallbacks — but its judgment was a sloth with an agenda. The transcript shows it exactly as it happened, which is the point of the architecture below: the model's opinions are suggestions; the deterministic layer holds the guarantees. How it works Deliberately boring architecture, because boring ships: Parsing (stdlib only): every non-empty line is a task; # comments and bullet/checkbox markers are stripped. My sample file's header comment got triaged as a task in the first build — fixed, and there's a test for it now. Judgment ( slothplan/llm.py ): one verdict per task from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Apache 2.0 open weights, Q4_K_M quantized) through the llama.cpp binary (MIT). Greedy decoding, ~3 seconds per item on two CPU cores. The model emits a single bucket word plus a short reason — a shape small enough for a 0.5B model to hold. This was a discovery , not the plan: my first prototype asked for one big JSON object covering all tasks, and the model hallucinated item numbers 13–20 for a 12-item list and stuffed 12 entries into a 3-item bucket. So the model judges one task at a time, and structure is enforced by code. Enforcement ( slothplan/triage.py ): every verdict is parsed and validated. Max 3 in "today" — overflow is moved to defer with the reason printed , so the cap is visible, not silent. Unparseable verdicts fall back to keyword rules and are labeled as fallback in the output . Nothing fails silently, ever. Zero third-party Python dependencies. Python 3.8, two downloaded files, and it runs. 29 unit tests, all passing. Why open innovation matters This tool cannot exist on a closed API, for two reasons — one practical, one philosophical. Practically: SlothPlan's entire design is a bet that a small model is enough. A 0.5B model is honest about what it is — opinionated, sometimes wrong, occasionally deleting your electricity bill — and the whole architecture (deterministic guardrails, labeled fallbacks, a --no-llm mode) is built around that honesty. You can only build that way if you can run the model locally, iterate on prompts for free at 3 a.m., and ship something whose marginal cost per triage is exactly zero. A closed API charges per token, which means every design decision bends toward fewer, bigger calls — the opposite of this architecture. And a to-do list is personal enough that "send it to someone's cloud" was never on the table. Philosophically: the open-weights ecosystem is what lets a student with a $0 budget and a borrowed VM build something in a day that would have been a research project five years ago. Qwen2.5's weights are public under Apache 2.0. llama.cpp is MIT. My code is MIT. Anyone can audit every layer, swap in a bigger GGUF with one flag, or fork the whole thing. That composability — weights, engine, and app all inspectable and replaceable — is open innovation working exactly as advertised. The moat isn't the model; it's the trust that comes from everything being auditable. Honest limitations I'd rather tell you than have you discover them: The bundled model is 0.5 billion parameters — tiny on purpose, so it runs on any laptop CPU. Its verdicts are opinions , and sometimes bad ones (see: the electricity bill incident). Any GGUF drops in via --model ; a bigger model would judge better. Reasons are sometimes missing ( (no reason given) ) — the model often emits just the bucket word despite being shown examples. The rule-based fallback is keyword heuristics, not understanding. It won't catch "renew the thingy before the thing expires." Prototype built in a day for a challenge, not a hardened product. 24 items max per run, .txt input, CLI only. Bonus-points honesty: I have no first user yet — this was built for the challenge this week, starting Monday morning. The demo above is real output from the actual tool, and the limitations section is real too. Try it Repo: https://github.com/swarnnim/slothplan ./scripts/download-llamacpp.sh ./scripts/download-model.sh python3 -m slothplan triage -f sample_todos/messy.txt If you also have a 47-item list you're avoiding: what's the one task on it you'd secretly love an app to delete for you? That's the roadmap — a bigger delete bucket.
items.summary_html:
SlothPlan: the to-do list that does less

My entry for the Hacktoberfest Week 3 "Slow and Steady" challenge — built for International Sloth Day, with open-weight models, zero API costs, and a philosophy I'd actually live by.

The problem

My to-do list has 47 items. Yours probably does too. And here's the dirty secret of productivity culture: the list isn't the work. Triaging the list is the work — the staring, the re-ordering, the guilt-math of "is learning Spanish more important than calling the dentist?" I have spent entire Sunday mornings reorganizing tasks instead of doing them, which is just procrastination wearing a planner's clothes.

Every to-do app on the planet answers this with more features: priorities, tags, Eisenhower matrices, AI scheduling assistants that need your calendar, your email, your soul, and a $12/month subscription. They make the triage heavier. Nobody built the app that does the triage for you and then — this is the important part — tells you to do less.

So for "Slow and Steady" I built exactly that: a tool that rewards laziness by doing the one piece of work you were avoiding (deciding what matters), capping your day at three things, and granting you written permission to delete the rest.

What I built

SlothPlan — a command-line tool where you dump a messy to-do list and get back three buckets: DO TODAY (max 3, non-negotiable), DEFER (officially not today's problem), and DELETE (permission granted, let it go). Each item gets a one-line reason. The judgment comes from a local open-weight model; the guarantees come from deterministic code.

python3 -m slothplan triage -f my-messy-todos.txt

The twist, same as my Week 2 entry: the model, the inference engine, and all the code run on your own machine. No account. No API key. No subscription. Your to-do list — which is, let's be honest, a map of your anxieties — never touches a network.

The demo (real transcript, unedited)

I fed it a 12-item Tuesday dump. Here is what the recorded run produced (full transcript in the repo's demo-output.txt — nothing cherry-picked):

=== SLOTHPLAN triage ===
method: rule-based fallback (--no-llm was passed; no model was run)

DO TODAY (max 3) — your only decisions today:
  1. Pay electricity bill, due Friday or they cut the power
     -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event
  2. Reply to Priya about the wedding RSVP — deadline is tomorrow
     -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event
  3. Submit the Hacktoberfest Week 3 entry README tonight
     -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event

DEFER — officially not today's problem:
  4. Call dentist to reschedule the appointment
     -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy]
  12. Call mom back — she called twice today
     -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy]

DELETE — permission granted, let it go:
  10. Delete that crypto spam email from "DOUBLE YOUR COINS"
     -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost
  11. Reorganize my Netflix watchlist
     -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost

That's the deterministic mode (--no-llm), and it's the mode I'd actually use daily: three real obligations surfaced, the dentist and mom politely bounced by the cap with an explanation, and the crypto spam and the Netflix-watchlist reorganization sentenced to death. Twelve decisions I didn't have to make.

Now the confession, because the transcript has two runs and I'm not hiding the first one: when I let the 0.5B model judge all 12 items itself, it took "rewards laziness" as a personal mission. It deleted the electricity bill. It called buying milk "spam". It deleted calling my mother. Every verdict parsed cleanly — 12/12, zero fallbacks — but its judgment was a sloth with an agenda. The transcript shows it exactly as it happened, which is the point of the architecture below: the model's opinions are suggestions; the deterministic layer holds the guarantees.

How it works

Deliberately boring architecture, because boring ships:

  • Parsing (stdlib only): every non-empty line is a task; # comments and bullet/checkbox markers are stripped. My sample file's header comment got triaged as a task in the first build — fixed, and there's a test for it now.
  • Judgment (slothplan/llm.py): one verdict per task from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Apache 2.0 open weights, Q4_K_M quantized) through the llama.cpp binary (MIT). Greedy decoding, ~3 seconds per item on two CPU cores. The model emits a single bucket word plus a short reason — a shape small enough for a 0.5B model to hold. This was a discovery, not the plan: my first prototype asked for one big JSON object covering all tasks, and the model hallucinated item numbers 13–20 for a 12-item list and stuffed 12 entries into a 3-item bucket. So the model judges one task at a time, and structure is enforced by code.
  • Enforcement (slothplan/triage.py): every verdict is parsed and validated. Max 3 in "today" — overflow is moved to defer with the reason printed, so the cap is visible, not silent. Unparseable verdicts fall back to keyword rules and are labeled as fallback in the output. Nothing fails silently, ever.
  • Zero third-party Python dependencies. Python 3.8, two downloaded files, and it runs. 29 unit tests, all passing.
Why open innovation matters

This tool cannot exist on a closed API, for two reasons — one practical, one philosophical.

Practically: SlothPlan's entire design is a bet that a small model is enough. A 0.5B model is honest about what it is — opinionated, sometimes wrong, occasionally deleting your electricity bill — and the whole architecture (deterministic guardrails, labeled fallbacks, a --no-llm mode) is built around that honesty. You can only build that way if you can run the model locally, iterate on prompts for free at 3 a.m., and ship something whose marginal cost per triage is exactly zero. A closed API charges per token, which means every design decision bends toward fewer, bigger calls — the opposite of this architecture. And a to-do list is personal enough that "send it to someone's cloud" was never on the table.

Philosophically: the open-weights ecosystem is what lets a student with a $0 budget and a borrowed VM build something in a day that would have been a research project five years ago. Qwen2.5's weights are public under Apache 2.0. llama.cpp is MIT. My code is MIT. Anyone can audit every layer, swap in a bigger GGUF with one flag, or fork the whole thing. That composability — weights, engine, and app all inspectable and replaceable — is open innovation working exactly as advertised. The moat isn't the model; it's the trust that comes from everything being auditable.

Honest limitations

I'd rather tell you than have you discover them:

  • The bundled model is 0.5 billion parameters — tiny on purpose, so it runs on any laptop CPU. Its verdicts are opinions, and sometimes bad ones (see: the electricity bill incident). Any GGUF drops in via --model; a bigger model would judge better.
  • Reasons are sometimes missing ((no reason given)) — the model often emits just the bucket word despite being shown examples.
  • The rule-based fallback is keyword heuristics, not understanding. It won't catch "renew the thingy before the thing expires."
  • Prototype built in a day for a challenge, not a hardened product. 24 items max per run, .txt input, CLI only.

Bonus-points honesty: I have no first user yet — this was built for the challenge this week, starting Monday morning. The demo above is real output from the actual tool, and the limitations section is real too.

Try it

Repo: https://github.com/swarnnim/slothplan

./scripts/download-llamacpp.sh
./scripts/download-model.sh
python3 -m slothplan triage -f sample_todos/messy.txt

If you also have a 47-item list you're avoiding: what's the one task on it you'd secretly love an app to delete for you? That's the roadmap — a bigger delete bucket.

items.title: Your Go Service Gets a Third Front Door: An MCP Adapter That Never Touches the Domain
items.summary: Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub The ticket says: "Make refunds callable from the AI assistant." Your refund service already has two ways in. Support staff hit POST /orders/{id}/refund , and the on-call engineer runs shop refund A-100 --cents 4999 from a terminal. Now a coding agent or a chat client wants a third way in, and it speaks the Model Context Protocol . There are two ways this goes. In one, somebody adds jsonschema tags to the domain structs, threads an *mcp.CallToolRequest into the service layer "just for the metadata", and the refund rules now import an SDK. In the other, you write one new package next to the HTTP handler, and git diff --stat shows zero lines of production code changed under internal/domain and internal/app . This post builds the second one with the official MCP Go SDK , at v1.8.0 as I write this, down to a CI check that fails if the inner packages ever import it. The service you already have Here is the domain. It knows what a refund is and when one is allowed. It imports errors and nothing else. // internal/domain/order.go package domain import "errors" var ( ErrOrderNotFound = errors . New ( "order not found" ) ErrAlreadyRefunded = errors . New ( "order was already refunded" ) ErrInvalidAmount = errors . New ( "refund must be between 1 cent and the amount paid" ) ) type Order struct { ID string PaidCents int64 Refunded bool } func ( o * Order ) Refund ( cents int64 ) error { if o . Refunded { return ErrAlreadyRefunded } if cents < 1 || cents > o . PaidCents { return ErrInvalidAmount } o . Refunded = true return nil } The application layer owns two ports. Orders is the driven port, the storage the use case needs. Refunder is the driving port, the one every front door calls. // internal/app/refund.go package app import ( "context" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) // Orders is the driven port: storage the use case needs. type Orders interface { Get ( ctx context . Context , id string ) ( domain . Order , error ) Save ( ctx context . Context , o domain . Order ) error } // RefundOrder is the command every driving adapter builds. type RefundOrder struct { OrderID string Cents int64 } type Refunded struct { OrderID string Cents int64 } // Refunder is the driving port. HTTP, CLI and MCP call this. type Refunder interface { Refund ( ctx context . Context , c RefundOrder ) ( Refunded , error ) } The service is the only thing that implements it: // internal/app/refund.go (continued) type RefundService struct { Orders Orders } func ( s RefundService ) Refund ( ctx context . Context , c RefundOrder , ) ( Refunded , error ) { o , err := s . Orders . Get ( ctx , c . OrderID ) if err != nil { return Refunded {}, err } if err := o . Refund ( c . Cents ); err != nil { return Refunded {}, err } if err := s . Orders . Save ( ctx , o ); err != nil { return Refunded {}, err } return Refunded { OrderID : o . ID , Cents : c . Cents }, nil } The HTTP adapter decodes a JSON body, builds an app.RefundOrder , calls Refund , and translates domain errors into status codes. The translation is the only part worth showing, because the MCP adapter will need its own version of it: // internal/adapter/httpapi/status.go package httpapi import ( "errors" "net/http" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func statusFor ( err error ) int { switch { case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrOrderNotFound ) : return http . StatusNotFound case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrAlreadyRefunded ) : return http . StatusConflict case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrInvalidAmount ) : return http . StatusUnprocessableEntity } return http . StatusInternalServerError } The CLI adapter does the same thing with flags and exit codes. Two adapters, one port, and neither one is visible from internal/domain . The third adapter: an MCP tool handler An MCP server exposes tools. A client lists them, the model picks one, and the client sends tools/call with JSON arguments, as the tools section of the spec describes. In the Go SDK, mcp.AddTool registers a typed handler. The package docs say the input schema is inferred from the In type, descriptions come from jsonschema struct tags, and inputs are validated before your handler runs. Those struct tags are wire format, so they belong to the adapter. The domain Order has no json tags and it will not get jsonschema tags either. The adapter defines its own input and output types and copies fields across: // internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go package mcpserver import ( "context" "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp" "example.com/shop/internal/app" ) type refundIn struct { OrderID string `json:"order_id" jsonschema:"order to refund"` Cents int64 `json:"cents" jsonschema:"amount in cents"` } type refundOut struct { OrderID string `json:"order_id"` Cents int64 `json:"cents"` } type refundHandler = mcp . ToolHandlerFor [ refundIn , refundOut ] func New ( r app . Refunder ) * mcp . Server { s := mcp . NewServer ( & mcp . Implementation { Name : "shop" , Version : "v0.1.0" , }, nil ) mcp . AddTool ( s , & mcp . Tool { Name : "refund_order" , Description : "Refund a paid order once, " + "for at most the amount paid." , }, refund ( r )) return s } The handler is a translator and nothing more: // internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go (continued) func refund ( r app . Refunder ) refundHandler { return func ( ctx context . Context , _ * mcp . CallToolRequest , in refundIn , ) ( * mcp . CallToolResult , refundOut , error ) { res , err := r . Refund ( ctx , app . RefundOrder { OrderID : in . OrderID , Cents : in . Cents , }) if err != nil { return nil , refundOut {}, toolError ( err ) } out := refundOut { OrderID : res . OrderID , Cents : res . Cents } return nil , out , nil } } Look at what New takes: app.Refunder , the same interface the HTTP handler takes. The handler ignores the *mcp.CallToolRequest . If you ever need something from it, such as the caller's client info, read it here and pass a plain value into the command. Do not pass the request type inward. Returning a nil result with a typed out is fine. In the SDK source , a nil result is replaced with an empty one, the output is marshaled into StructuredContent , and a JSON text copy goes into Content , which matches the spec's advice that structured results also ship as text for older clients. Domain errors become tool errors, not protocol errors The spec defines two kinds of failure . Protocol errors are JSON-RPC errors for unknown tools, malformed requests and server faults. Tool execution errors come back as a normal result with isError: true , and they cover business logic errors like "already refunded". The spec says clients SHOULD pass tool execution errors to the model so it can self-correct. That maps neatly onto the HTTP split between a 409 and a 500. "Order was already refunded" is information the model can act on: stop, or tell the user. A database timeout is not, and its text may contain a host name or a query you do not want in a model's context. The SDK does the plumbing. When a ToolHandlerFor returns an ordinary Go error, the CallToolResult docs say IsError is set and the error string goes into Content as text. Only a *jsonrpc.Error is sent as a protocol error, per the server code . So the adapter's job is to decide which error text the model is allowed to read: // internal/adapter/mcpserver/errors.go package mcpserver import ( "errors" "log" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func toolError ( err error ) error { switch { case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrOrderNotFound ), errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrAlreadyRefunded ), errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrInvalidAmount ) : return err } log . Printf ( "refund_order: %v" , err ) return errors . New ( "internal error" ) } The log.Printf is deliberate. Over stdio, the spec says the server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, and MAY log to stderr. Go's default logger writes to standard error , so it is safe. A stray fmt.Println in an adapter is not: it corrupts the message stream. The binary is a few lines of wiring. Here the in-memory store stands in for your real Postgres adapter: // cmd/shop-mcp/main.go package main import ( "context" "log" "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/mcpserver" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore" "example.com/shop/internal/app" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func main () { orders := memstore . New ( domain . Order { ID : "A-100" , PaidCents : 4999 }) svc := app . RefundService { Orders : orders } srv := mcpserver . New ( svc ) ctx := context . Background () if err := srv . Run ( ctx , & mcp . StdioTransport {}); err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } } To try it from Claude Code, build it and register it as a local stdio server with claude mcp add : go get github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk@v1.8.0 go build -o bin/shop-mcp ./cmd/shop-mcp claude mcp add --transport stdio shop -- " $PWD /bin/shop-mcp" Prove the domain stayed clean "We didn't touch the domain" is a claim. Make it a check. go list -deps walks a package and everything it imports, as the go command docs describe. Run it on the inner packages and grep for anything that should not be there: # from the module root; fails if go list fails or anything matches deps = $( go list -deps ./internal/domain ./internal/app ) && ! grep -E 'modelcontextprotocol|/adapter/' <<< " $deps " go.mod did change, because the module now requires the SDK. The domain's dependency list did not. That is the distinction this check enforces. A stricter version lives in the domain package as a test. go list -json reports a Standard field on every package, true for the standard library, so the test fails if the domain depends on anything outside the standard library except itself: // internal/domain/imports_test.go package domain_test import ( "bytes" "encoding/json" "os/exec" "testing" ) const self = "example.com/shop/internal/domain" func TestDomainImportsOnlyStdlib ( t * testing . T ) { cmd := exec . Command ( "go" , "list" , "-deps" , "-json" , "." ) out , err := cmd . Output () if err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } dec := json . NewDecoder ( bytes . NewReader ( out )) for dec . More () { var p struct { ImportPath string Standard bool } if err := dec . Decode ( & p ); err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } if ! p . Standard && p . ImportPath != self { t . Errorf ( "domain depends on %s" , p . ImportPath ) } } } The . works because go test runs each test binary from inside the package's source directory. And because the command has no -test flag, go list reports the package itself rather than its test binary, so the test's own imports ( os/exec , encoding/json ) are not part of what it checks. Test the use case through the fake, then the adapter in memory The fake is a driven adapter that keeps orders in a map. It implements app.Orders and returns the domain's not-found error: // internal/adapter/memstore/orders.go package memstore import ( "context" "sync" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) type Orders struct { mu sync . Mutex m map [ string ] domain . Order } func New ( seed ... domain . Order ) * Orders { s := & Orders { m : make ( map [ string ] domain . Order )} for _ , o := range seed { s . m [ o . ID ] = o } return s } func ( s * Orders ) Get ( _ context . Context , id string , ) ( domain . Order , error ) { s . mu . Lock () defer s . mu . Unlock () o , ok := s . m [ id ] if ! ok { return domain . Order {}, domain . ErrOrderNotFound } return o , nil } func ( s * Orders ) Save ( _ context . Context , o domain . Order ) error { s . mu . Lock () defer s . mu . Unlock () s . m [ o . ID ] = o return nil } The use case test runs steps in order against one order, because the second refund depends on the first: // internal/app/refund_test.go package app_test import ( "context" "errors" "testing" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore" "example.com/shop/internal/app" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func TestRefund ( t * testing . T ) { ctx := context . Background () orders := memstore . New ( domain . Order { ID : "A-1" , PaidCents : 500 }) svc := app . RefundService { Orders : orders } steps := [] struct { id string cents int64 want error }{ { "missing" , 100 , domain . ErrOrderNotFound }, { "A-1" , 501 , domain . ErrInvalidAmount }, { "A-1" , 0 , domain . ErrInvalidAmount }, { "A-1" , 200 , nil }, { "A-1" , 100 , domain . ErrAlreadyRefunded }, } for _ , s := range steps { _ , err := svc . Refund ( ctx , app . RefundOrder { OrderID : s . id , Cents : s . cents , }) if ! errors . Is ( err , s . want ) { t . Errorf ( "Refund(%s, %d) = %v, want %v" , s . id , s . cents , err , s . want ) } } } No MCP anywhere in it. That test was true before the third door existed and it stays true after. The adapter gets its own test, over the SDK's in-memory transports so no process is spawned. The package examples connect the server to one end of NewInMemoryTransports and a client to the other. The assertion is the one that matters for agents: a missing order comes back as a tool result with IsError set, not as a protocol failure. // internal/adapter/mcpserver/server_test.go package mcpserver_test import ( "context" "testing" "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/mcpserver" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore" "example.com/shop/internal/app" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func TestUnknownOrderIsToolError ( t * testing . T ) { ctx := context . Background () svc := app . RefundService { Orders : memstore . New ()} st , ct := mcp . NewInMemoryTransports () _ , err := mcpserver . New ( svc ) . Connect ( ctx , st , nil ) if err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } c := mcp . NewClient ( & mcp . Implementation { Name : "test" , Version : "v0" , }, nil ) cs , err := c . Connect ( ctx , ct , nil ) if err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } defer cs . Close () res , err := cs . CallTool ( ctx , & mcp . CallToolParams { Name : "refund_order" , Arguments : map [ string ] any { "order_id" : "nope" , "cents" : 100 , }, }) if err != nil { t . Fatalf ( "got a protocol error: %v" , err ) } if ! res . IsError { t . Fatal ( "want IsError on the tool result" ) } text := res . Content [ 0 ] . ( * mcp . TextContent ) . Text if text != domain . ErrOrderNotFound . Error () { t . Fatalf ( "model would read %q" , text ) } } What the diff looks like Count the files. The ticket says: "Make refunds callable from the AI assistant." Your refund service already has two ways in. Support staff hit POST /orders/{id}/refund, and the on-call engineer runs shop refund A-100 --cents 4999 from a terminal. Now a coding agent or a chat client wants a third way in, and it speaks the Model Context Protocol.

There are two ways this goes. In one, somebody adds jsonschema tags to the domain structs, threads an *mcp.CallToolRequest into the service layer "just for the metadata", and the refund rules now import an SDK. In the other, you write one new package next to the HTTP handler, and git diff --stat shows zero lines of production code changed under internal/domain and internal/app.

This post builds the second one with the official MCP Go SDK, at v1.8.0 as I write this, down to a CI check that fails if the inner packages ever import it.

The service you already have

Here is the domain. It knows what a refund is and when one is allowed. It imports errors and nothing else.

// internal/domain/order.go
package domain

import "errors"

var (
    ErrOrderNotFound   = errors.New("order not found")
    ErrAlreadyRefunded = errors.New("order was already refunded")
    ErrInvalidAmount   = errors.New(
        "refund must be between 1 cent and the amount paid")
)

type Order struct {
    ID        string
    PaidCents int64
    Refunded  bool
}

func (o *Order) Refund(cents int64) error {
    if o.Refunded {
        return ErrAlreadyRefunded
    }
    if cents < 1 || cents > o.PaidCents {
        return ErrInvalidAmount
    }
    o.Refunded = true
    return nil
}

The application layer owns two ports. Orders is the driven port, the storage the use case needs. Refunder is the driving port, the one every front door calls.

// internal/app/refund.go
package app

import (
    "context"

    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

// Orders is the driven port: storage the use case needs.
type Orders interface {
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (domain.Order, error)
    Save(ctx context.Context, o domain.Order) error
}

// RefundOrder is the command every driving adapter builds.
type RefundOrder struct {
    OrderID string
    Cents   int64
}

type Refunded struct {
    OrderID string
    Cents   int64
}

// Refunder is the driving port. HTTP, CLI and MCP call this.
type Refunder interface {
    Refund(ctx context.Context, c RefundOrder) (Refunded, error)
}

The service is the only thing that implements it:

// internal/app/refund.go (continued)
type RefundService struct{ Orders Orders }

func (s RefundService) Refund(
    ctx context.Context, c RefundOrder,
) (Refunded, error) {
    o, err := s.Orders.Get(ctx, c.OrderID)
    if err != nil {
        return Refunded{}, err
    }
    if err := o.Refund(c.Cents); err != nil {
        return Refunded{}, err
    }
    if err := s.Orders.Save(ctx, o); err != nil {
        return Refunded{}, err
    }
    return Refunded{OrderID: o.ID, Cents: c.Cents}, nil
}

The HTTP adapter decodes a JSON body, builds an app.RefundOrder, calls Refund, and translates domain errors into status codes. The translation is the only part worth showing, because the MCP adapter will need its own version of it:

// internal/adapter/httpapi/status.go
package httpapi

import (
    "errors"
    "net/http"

    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

func statusFor(err error) int {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrOrderNotFound):
        return http.StatusNotFound
    case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrAlreadyRefunded):
        return http.StatusConflict
    case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrInvalidAmount):
        return http.StatusUnprocessableEntity
    }
    return http.StatusInternalServerError
}

The CLI adapter does the same thing with flags and exit codes. Two adapters, one port, and neither one is visible from internal/domain.

The third adapter: an MCP tool handler

An MCP server exposes tools. A client lists them, the model picks one, and the client sends tools/call with JSON arguments, as the tools section of the spec describes. In the Go SDK, mcp.AddTool registers a typed handler. The package docs say the input schema is inferred from the In type, descriptions come from jsonschema struct tags, and inputs are validated before your handler runs.

Those struct tags are wire format, so they belong to the adapter. The domain Order has no json tags and it will not get jsonschema tags either. The adapter defines its own input and output types and copies fields across:

// internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go
package mcpserver

import (
    "context"

    "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp"

    "example.com/shop/internal/app"
)

type refundIn struct {
    OrderID string `json:"order_id" jsonschema:"order to refund"`
    Cents   int64  `json:"cents" jsonschema:"amount in cents"`
}

type refundOut struct {
    OrderID string `json:"order_id"`
    Cents   int64  `json:"cents"`
}

type refundHandler = mcp.ToolHandlerFor[refundIn, refundOut]

func New(r app.Refunder) *mcp.Server {
    s := mcp.NewServer(&mcp.Implementation{
        Name: "shop", Version: "v0.1.0",
    }, nil)
    mcp.AddTool(s, &mcp.Tool{
        Name: "refund_order",
        Description: "Refund a paid order once, " +
            "for at most the amount paid.",
    }, refund(r))
    return s
}

The handler is a translator and nothing more:

// internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go (continued)
func refund(r app.Refunder) refundHandler {
    return func(
        ctx context.Context, _ *mcp.CallToolRequest, in refundIn,
    ) (*mcp.CallToolResult, refundOut, error) {
        res, err := r.Refund(ctx, app.RefundOrder{
            OrderID: in.OrderID,
            Cents:   in.Cents,
        })
        if err != nil {
            return nil, refundOut{}, toolError(err)
        }
        out := refundOut{OrderID: res.OrderID, Cents: res.Cents}
        return nil, out, nil
    }
}

Look at what New takes: app.Refunder, the same interface the HTTP handler takes. The handler ignores the *mcp.CallToolRequest. If you ever need something from it, such as the caller's client info, read it here and pass a plain value into the command. Do not pass the request type inward.

Returning a nil result with a typed out is fine. In the SDK source, a nil result is replaced with an empty one, the output is marshaled into StructuredContent, and a JSON text copy goes into Content, which matches the spec's advice that structured results also ship as text for older clients.

Domain errors become tool errors, not protocol errors

The spec defines two kinds of failure. Protocol errors are JSON-RPC errors for unknown tools, malformed requests and server faults. Tool execution errors come back as a normal result with isError: true, and they cover business logic errors like "already refunded". The spec says clients SHOULD pass tool execution errors to the model so it can self-correct.

That maps neatly onto the HTTP split between a 409 and a 500. "Order was already refunded" is information the model can act on: stop, or tell the user. A database timeout is not, and its text may contain a host name or a query you do not want in a model's context.

The SDK does the plumbing. When a ToolHandlerFor returns an ordinary Go error, the CallToolResult docs say IsError is set and the error string goes into Content as text. Only a *jsonrpc.Error is sent as a protocol error, per the server code. So the adapter's job is to decide which error text the model is allowed to read:

// internal/adapter/mcpserver/errors.go
package mcpserver

import (
    "errors"
    "log"

    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

func toolError(err error) error {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrOrderNotFound),
        errors.Is(err, domain.ErrAlreadyRefunded),
        errors.Is(err, domain.ErrInvalidAmount):
        return err
    }
    log.Printf("refund_order: %v", err)
    return errors.New("internal error")
}

The log.Printf is deliberate. Over stdio, the spec says the server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, and MAY log to stderr. Go's default logger writes to standard error, so it is safe. A stray fmt.Println in an adapter is not: it corrupts the message stream.

// cmd/shop-mcp/main.go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"

    "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp"

    "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/mcpserver"
    "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore"
    "example.com/shop/internal/app"
    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

func main() {
    orders := memstore.New(domain.Order{ID: "A-100", PaidCents: 4999})
    svc := app.RefundService{Orders: orders}
    srv := mcpserver.New(svc)
    ctx := context.Background()
    if err := srv.Run(ctx, &mcp.StdioTransport{}); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

go get github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk@v1.8.0
go build -o bin/shop-mcp ./cmd/shop-mcp
claude mcp add --transport stdio shop -- "$PWD/bin/shop-mcp"

"We didn't touch the domain" is a claim. Make it a check. go list -deps walks a package and everything it imports, as the go command docs describe. Run it on the inner packages and grep for anything that should not be there:

# from the module root; fails if go list fails or anything matches
deps=$(go list -deps ./internal/domain ./internal/app) &&
  ! grep -E 'modelcontextprotocol|/adapter/' <<<"$deps"

go.mod did change, because the module now requires the SDK. The domain's dependency list did not. That is the distinction this check enforces.

// internal/domain/imports_test.go
package domain_test

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "os/exec"
    "testing"
)

const self = "example.com/shop/internal/domain"

func TestDomainImportsOnlyStdlib(t *testing.T) {
    cmd := exec.Command("go", "list", "-deps", "-json", ".")
    out, err := cmd.Output()
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    dec := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(out))
    for dec.More() {
        var p struct {
            ImportPath string
            Standard   bool
        }
        if err := dec.Decode(&p); err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        if !p.Standard && p.ImportPath != self {
            t.Errorf("domain depends on %s", p.ImportPath)
        }
    }
}

The . works because go test runs each test binary from inside the package's source directory. And because the command has no -test flag, go list reports the package itself rather than its test binary, so the test's own imports (os/exec, encoding/json) are not part of what it checks.

The fake is a driven adapter that keeps orders in a map. It implements app.Orders and returns the domain's not-found error:

// internal/adapter/memstore/orders.go
package memstore

import (
    "context"
    "sync"

    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

type Orders struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    m  map[string]domain.Order
}

func New(seed ...domain.Order) *Orders {
    s := &Orders{m: make(map[string]domain.Order)}
    for _, o := range seed {
        s.m[o.ID] = o
    }
    return s
}

func (s *Orders) Get(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (domain.Order, error) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()
    o, ok := s.m[id]
    if !ok {
        return domain.Order{}, domain.ErrOrderNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (s *Orders) Save(_ context.Context, o domain.Order) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()
    s.m[o.ID] = o
    return nil
}

The use case test runs steps in order against one order, because the second refund depends on the first:

// internal/app/refund_test.go
package app_test

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "testing"

    "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore"
    "example.com/shop/internal/app"
    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

func TestRefund(t *testing.T) {
    ctx := context.Background()
    orders := memstore.New(domain.Order{ID: "A-1", PaidCents: 500})
    svc := app.RefundService{Orders: orders}

    steps := []struct {
        id    string
        cents int64
        want  error
    }{
        {"missing", 100, domain.ErrOrderNotFound},
        {"A-1", 501, domain.ErrInvalidAmount},
        {"A-1", 0, domain.ErrInvalidAmount},
        {"A-1", 200, nil},
        {"A-1", 100, domain.ErrAlreadyRefunded},
    }
    for _, s := range steps {
        _, err := svc.Refund(ctx, app.RefundOrder{
            OrderID: s.id, Cents: s.cents,
        })
        if !errors.Is(err, s.want) {
            t.Errorf("Refund(%s, %d) = %v, want %v",
                s.id, s.cents, err, s.want)
        }
    }
}

No MCP anywhere in it. That test was true before the third door existed and it stays true after.

// internal/adapter/mcpserver/server_test.go
package mcpserver_test

import (
    "context"
    "testing"

    "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp"

    "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/mcpserver"
    "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore"
    "example.com/shop/internal/app"
    "example.com/shop/internal/domain"
)

func TestUnknownOrderIsToolError(t *testing.T) {
    ctx := context.Background()
    svc := app.RefundService{Orders: memstore.New()}
    st, ct := mcp.NewInMemoryTransports()
    _, err := mcpserver.New(svc).Connect(ctx, st, nil)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    c := mcp.NewClient(&mcp.Implementation{
        Name: "test", Version: "v0",
    }, nil)
    cs, err := c.Connect(ctx, ct, nil)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer cs.Close()

    res, err := cs.CallTool(ctx, &mcp.CallToolParams{
        Name: "refund_order",
        Arguments: map[string]any{
            "order_id": "nope", "cents": 100,
        },
    })
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("got a protocol error: %v", err)
    }
    if !res.IsError {
        t.Fatal("want IsError on the tool result")
    }
    text := res.Content[0].(*mcp.TextContent).Text
    if text != domain.ErrOrderNotFound.Error() {
        t.Fatalf("model would read %q", text)
    }
}

items.title: Your AI Tool Will Change Mid-Contract: The Exit-Clause Checklist to Sign With
items.summary: The product you bought has a shipping schedule now For most of software history, the thing you signed a contract for was the thing you got. This month is a useful illustration of why that assumption no longer holds. OpenAI's Codex team announced 28 consecutive days of shipping: every single day bringing either a clear improvement for users "or a full reset." Prediction features landed on day five. A 500,000-token context window arrived on day seven. The other major labs spent the same stretch shipping their own waves of new models and features. Vendors frame this as a gift, and often it is. Read it as a buyer and it says something else: the product you evaluate during a trial is not the product you'll be running at renewal. Classic SaaS shipped a few times a year, with release notes and migration windows. AI tools change the model underneath, the usage limits, and sometimes the price — weekly, by design, with the vendor explicitly reserving the right to "reset." The standard small-business response is a shrug: tech moves fast, nothing to be done. The shrug is where the money leaks. When the product can change monthly, the only stable thing in the relationship is the contract — and the only term that protects you from a change you didn't choose is the exit clause. It's the one term written for the world the vendor is describing out loud. The exit-clause checklist Run this before signing anything new, and bring it to every renewal — the renewal is where you have actual leverage. Five items. 1. Data export in a usable format — tested, not promised Nearly every tool says "you can export your data." What matters is what that means: machine-readable CSV or JSON, covering your inputs, uploaded documents, generated outputs, and your custom instructions or workflows — not a PDF of your settings page. Then test the export during the trial, not during the breakup. Create three records, hit export, open the file. If export is ugly while things are good, it will be worse while things are bad. 2. A post-termination access window, in writing Standard terms across the market give you anywhere from zero to 90 days to retrieve your data after cancellation — and that range is real, not theoretical. What good looks like: export stays available for at least 30 days after termination, nothing gets deleted inside that window, and retrieval isn't charged. If the standard terms don't say it, ask before you sign. If the answer is "call support," you've just learned what your data's exit looks like. 3. Notice and a remedy when the product changes mid-term The AI-specific term, and the one almost nobody asks about. Two questions: how much notice do you get when the underlying model, price, or usage limits change — and what's the remedy if a feature you pay for is removed or degraded mid-term? Reasonable asks: advance notice of material changes, plus a downgrade-or-exit right — a pro-rated refund or penalty-free cancellation — if a change takes away what you signed up for. A vendor willing to "reset" the product on any given Tuesday should be able to answer that in one sentence. Vague silence tells you who eats the risk. 4. Every access point, and a way to revoke them An AI subscription is rarely one login. It's OAuth grants to your Google or Microsoft account, API keys your automations run on, browser extensions, connected integrations, sub-agents with their own permissions. Each one is a door that stays open after you cancel. Ask for documentation of every access the tool takes and a revocation path for each — then make "revoke all access" a named step in your offboarding. A cancelled subscription with live credentials is a security hole and a recurring charge waiting to be rediscovered. 5. What the tool learned — yours and portable If the assistant holds your custom instructions, learned workflows, and memory, the expensive part of leaving isn't the records — it's the context. Ask whether prompts, configurations, and memory export. If they don't, run the discipline that makes the question moot: write your processes in your own files and let the tool read them. Then an exit never costs you the knowledge, and the answer to "who owns the workflow" stops mattering. The honest boundary Custom contract terms need leverage, and leverage needs spend. Nobody is redlining your exit rights on a $30-a-month self-serve plan, and a checklist that pretends otherwise wastes your evening. At the low end, this list is a verification list: read the standard terms before you adopt, score the tool on the five items, and walk away from the ones that fail. The moment you're signing anything annual, per-seat, or four figures — that's when you send the list and expect written answers. The 10-minute quarterly review For tools already in your stack, the contract moment has passed — so the discipline shifts to a review. Once a quarter, per tool, ten minutes, five questions: Still the right tool? Knowing what you know now, would you adopt this today? What changed since last quarter — price, limits, model, features? Which of those changes did you actually choose? Does the export still work? Run it. Export formats change more often than contracts do. What access does it hold right now? List the integrations and keys. Revoke the dead ones. When is renewal, and what would leaving cost? Do the exit math before the auto-charge does it for you. Question three is the one everyone skips and the one that saves the most grief — it converts "I think we could export if we needed to" into a fact you checked this quarter. What not to do Don't sign multi-year AI contracts right now — not even for the discount. The discount is priced for a stability this market no longer sells. Annual at most, and only where the checklist passes. Don't confuse exporting data with exporting the workflow. Records are the easy part. Instructions, memory, and learned context are what actually trap you. Don't read the terms for the first time when you're unhappy. The exit clause is worth the most on the day you're happiest — that's the day the vendor still has to compete for you. One line to keep In the last era of software, stability was part of what you bought. In this one, the change rate is the product. The exit clause is the only term that prices that honestly — so read it first, test it first, and negotiate it first. If you want the full framework for making any agent earn its seat — the permission ladder, the boring first assignment, and the one-page process format that keeps your context portable and your exits cheap — it's all written down in The AI Agent Owner's Playbook . $49 CAD, instant download.

  2. What changed since last quarter — price, limits, model, features? Which of those changes did you actually choose?
  3. Does the export still work? Run it. Export formats change more often than contracts do.
  4. What access does it hold right now? List the integrations and keys. Revoke the dead ones.
  5. When is renewal, and what would leaving cost? Do the exit math before the auto-charge does it for you.

Question three is the one everyone skips and the one that saves the most grief — it converts "I think we could export if we needed to" into a fact you checked this quarter.

What not to do
  • Don't sign multi-year AI contracts right now — not even for the discount. The discount is priced for a stability this market no longer sells. Annual at most, and only where the checklist passes.
  • Don't confuse exporting data with exporting the workflow. Records are the easy part. Instructions, memory, and learned context are what actually trap you.
  • Don't read the terms for the first time when you're unhappy. The exit clause is worth the most on the day you're happiest — that's the day the vendor still has to compete for you.
One line to keep

In the last era of software, stability was part of what you bought. In this one, the change rate is the product. The exit clause is the only term that prices that honestly — so read it first, test it first, and negotiate it first.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

LazyDesk AI is a local-first, privacy-first desktop file organizer powered by open-weight AI.

We all know the pain: you download invoices, lecture notes, research PDFs, client agreements, data sheets, and screenshots throughout the week. Before long, your Downloads or Desktop folder is a digital wasteland of cryptic filenames like INV-98234-billing-oct.txt, CS204_Fall2024_Syllabus.pdf, screenshot_dashboard_v1.png, and Freelance_Consulting_Agreement_Draft.docx.

Sorting, renaming, and categorizing them manually is mind-numbing busywork—so we procrastinate and let the clutter grow.

LazyDesk AI solves this by automating the boring work completely on your local machine:

  1. Scans a target folder within strict, user-permitted directory perimeters.
  2. Extracts document text locally (from PDFs, Word DOCX documents, Markdown notes, CSVs, and image metadata) without sending anything to a cloud API.
  3. Infers file purpose and contents using local open-weight AI (via Ollama, supporting Qwen3, Llama 3.1, or any local GGUF model).
  4. Proposes standardized filenames and destination folders (Finance, Work, Education, Projects, Documents, Images, Notes, Other).
  5. Requires explicit review and approval: Nothing is moved silently. You can edit proposed names inline, swap categories, or exclude files.
  6. Previews the exact filesystem paths: Displays source and destination paths with collision detection (non-destructive suffixes like Invoice (1).txt ensure no files are ever overwritten).
  7. Executes safe moves and logs cryptographic SHA-256 hashes: Supports instant, one-click undo if you ever want to revert an organization batch.

Who gets to be lazier?
Students, freelancers, software engineers, and office workers who want a clean, structured workspace without spending their Sunday afternoons manually renaming files.

Check out the full GitHub repository and run it locally in minutes:

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.

1. Product Overview

LazyDesk AI is a local-first, privacy-respecting intelligent file organizer.

Every day, developers, students, freelancers, and office workers end up with cluttered "Downloads", "Desktop", and project directories filled with cryptically named files like INV-98234-billing-oct.txt, CS204_Fall2024_Syllabus.pdf, screenshot_dashboard_v1.png, and Freelance_Consulting_Agreement_Draft.docx. Sorting, renaming, and filing them manually is tedious and procrastinated on.

LazyDesk AI automates this repetitive chore using open-weight local AI (via Ollama):

  1. Scans a permitted folder on your local drive.
  2. Safely extracts text summaries locally from PDFs, Word DOCX documents, Markdown notes, CSVs, and image metadata.
  3. Infers purpose using local open-weight models (such as qwen3 or llama3.1).
  4. Suggests clear, standardized filenames and destination categories (Finance, Work, Education…
View on GitHub

The complete project is open-source under the MIT License.

Tech Stack
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, React Router, Lucide React icons.
  • Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, Uvicorn.
  • Document Processing: PyMuPDF (pymupdf) for PDFs, python-docx for Word documents, Pillow (PIL) for image metadata, and built-in Python I/O for text, Markdown, and CSV.
  • Local AI: Ollama REST API (http://localhost:11434) running open-weight models (Qwen3 default, Llama 3.1 fallback), plus deterministic smart mock mode for testing and low-resource environments.
  • Testing: pytest automated test suite with 13 comprehensive unit/integration tests and complete mock AI coverage.
How I Built It 1. Zero-Cloud Privacy & Local Inference

Commercial AI APIs (like OpenAI or Anthropic) charge per token and require uploading file contents to third-party cloud servers. For personal bank statements, client contracts, and student homework, sending documents to a remote cloud is a privacy non-starter.

LazyDesk AI connects exclusively to a local Ollama instance. Document text is extracted in memory using PyMuPDF and python-docx, bounded to 4,000 characters, and sent to localhost:11434. The model outputs a structured JSON response specifying:

  • description: 1-sentence summary of document purpose
  • suggested_filename: Clean, descriptive base name without file extensions or illegal characters
  • category: Whitelisted folder category (Documents, Education, Work, Finance, Projects, Images, Notes, Other)
  • reason: Justification based on detected content
2. Treating AI Output as Untrusted

LLMs can hallucinate file paths or produce invalid operating system characters. LazyDesk AI treats all model output as untrusted user input:

  • Paths are never generated directly by the LLM. Destination paths are strictly assembled by the backend from validated category whitelists and sanitized filenames.
  • Filename sanitization removes reserved Windows device names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL), strips illegal characters (\ / : * ? " < > |), and guarantees original extensions are preserved.
3. Filesystem Security Perimeter

To prevent arbitrary path traversal or accidental deletion:

  • The backend enforces ALLOWED_ROOTS. Every target path is checked using os.path.realpath to confirm it resolves inside an allowed directory.
  • Symbolic links and directory traversal sequences (.., \0) are rejected.
  • Files are never overwritten: If Invoice.pdf exists, the destination automatically becomes Invoice (1).pdf.
4. Hash-Checked Transactional Undo

Every executed move records the original source path, destination path, execution timestamp, and cryptographic SHA-256 checksum in SQLite. When undo is triggered:

  • The system verifies that the file is still present at the destination.
  • It computes the current hash to ensure the file has not been altered since organization.
  • It verifies that the original location is free before moving the file back safely.
Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open-source and open-weight AI (like Qwen, Llama, Mistral, and the Ollama ecosystem) made LazyDesk AI possible in ways proprietary cloud APIs never could:

  1. Zero Marginal Cost for Utility Software: Running a cloud LLM every time a user downloads a batch of files would require recurring subscriptions or API credit management. With open-weight models, once downloaded, file analysis is free and unlimited forever.
  2. True Data Sovereignty: Personal tax returns, paystubs, medical documents, and proprietary project roadmaps should not leave the user's hard drive. Open innovation brings the AI model to the data, rather than sending the data to the AI.
  3. Offline Resilience: LazyDesk AI runs completely offline on planes, trains, or low-connectivity environments. If a GPU daemon is unavailable, the smart deterministic heuristic kicks in without breaking the workflow.
  4. Community Control: Developers can swap in specialized domain models (e.g., medical, legal, or code-specific weights) with a single environment variable change.
My Agent Session

This application was engineered, tested, and polished collaboratively using the Google DeepMind Antigravity IDE agent session. The session history spans full-stack architecture design, defensive filesystem security rules, PyMuPDF and python-docx integration, Ollama structured JSON prompt engineering, automated pytest test suite creation, and live browser automation.

The Lazy Payoff The Problem

During development, we tested LazyDesk AI against a folder of 20+ cluttered, realistically simulated files (invoices, academic course syllabi, engineering design docs, contractor agreements, expense CSVs, and project notes).

The Manual Benchmark
  • Opening each file to inspect contents: ~15–30 seconds per file.
  • Thinking of a standardized naming convention: ~10 seconds.
  • Creating destination folders and moving the file: ~10 seconds.
  • Total Manual Effort: ~15–20 minutes of tedious, error-prone clicking for a single folder.
The LazyDesk AI Benchmark
  • Click Scan Folder: 0.2 seconds.
  • Click Analyze with Local AI: ~5–8 seconds for the entire batch.
  • Click Preview & Execute: 1 second.
  • Total LazyDesk Effort: Under 15 seconds, zero files sent to cloud servers, and full ability to revert with one click.

items.title: We Requested Indexing on 10 Pages Today. One Came Back Rejected — by Our Own Header.
items.summary: Our site has an indexing gap: 2,478 known pages, 208 indexed. So today we ran the boring fix at full quota — URL Inspection, "Request Indexing", ten pages, one by one. Nine went through: tested, queued for priority crawling. The tenth — our brand-new signup page — came back rejected, and the reason is worth more than the nine successes: noindex in an HTTP X-Robots-Tag header. Not a meta tag. Not robots.txt. The page fetched fine, was allowed to crawl, allowed to index — and the header quietly overruled all of it. Classic pattern: auth-adjacent pages (signup, login, account) get a blanket noindex from middleware, and one day the page you actually want ranking inherits it. Three checks that catch it in a minute: curl -sI https://yoursite.com/page | grep -i robots — see the header directly URL Inspection in Search Console — the page-indexing section names the exact blocker, in our case the X-Robots-Tag header Test the specific route, not the template — middleware rules apply per-route and bite where you least expect The meta lesson for us: we spent four days thinking the Request Indexing button was broken (it wasn't opening in our setup — that's another story). The tool worked; our process for using it didn't. Indexing tools fail quietly, in both directions. (For the record: of the nine queued pages — core /app/ routes — one had been crawled but never indexed; the other eight were discovered and never crawled. Requesting indexing doesn't guarantee inclusion; it puts them in a priority queue. The scoreboard is the indexed-page count, and we'll report it honestly whatever it does.) Check your signup page's headers before you assume Google is ignoring you. Ours was — because we told it to.

items.title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
items.summary: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back. items.title: Reward shaping slashes reasoning steps by 65%
items.summary: Tailored reinforcement‑learning rewards reactivate the dormant THINK circuitry in hybrid language models, chopping chain‑of‑thought traces by roughly two‑thirds without sacrificing answer quality. The surprise is that a modest reshaping of the reward signal does more than steer behavior—it resurrects an internal reasoning mode that the model already possessed. Before these studies, practitioners either forced models to emit full CoT sequences or relied on static heuristics that never touched the model’s latent THINK pathway. RL was popular for improving performance in the NO‑THINK regime, but its gains were credited to newly learned policies rather than to any reclamation of existing reasoning capacity. RLCD² lifts the share of reasoning traces that finish within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and slashes average trace length by as much as 65 % while largely preserving decision accuracy. At 9B parameters, termination climbs from 45.9 % to 93.9 %, and mean trace length drops from 2,494 to 868 tokens—a full 65 % reduction [1] . The think win rate surges from 50 % to 94 % for the 8B checkpoint, with comparable jumps to 86 % for 4B and 84 % for 1.7B, meaning that after RL training a response is judged more THINK‑like than an original NO‑THINK output in the overwhelming majority of pairwise comparisons [2] . “Original-to-RL patching of the think subspace lowers accuracy to 0.244, removing 75 % of the RL gain, and response length falls from 7.0k to 4.2k tokens while reflection words fall from 13.0 to 3.9 per response” – an experiment that directly ties the reward‑induced performance boost to a low‑dimensional THINK‑related activation subspace [2] . These results are confined to specific hybrid architectures (the Qwen3 series and StartLux‑Decision) and their respective benchmark suites—arithmetic and tool‑use evaluations for the Qwen3 experiments and decision benchmarks such as Decision Index and DecisionPivot for StartLux‑Decision—and it remains unclear whether the same reward shaping will transfer to pure decoder‑only models or to other task domains. Moreover, the reported “largely preserving accuracy” still masks modest drops that could matter for high‑stakes applications, suggesting a trade‑off curve that has not been fully mapped. If the 65 % reduction in reasoning steps holds across deployments, developers can slash inference latency and token‑processing costs by swapping in the publicly released LoRA adapters for the Qwen3 models (provided in the think‑leakage repository) that implement the reward‑shaping objective, without retraining the base model. This cheap post‑hoc tweak turns expensive chain‑of‑thought pipelines into leaner, faster decision engines. References StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions The Thinking Leakage in Reinforcement Learning for LLMs

Moreover, the reported “largely preserving accuracy” still masks modest drops that could matter for high‑stakes applications, suggesting a trade‑off curve that has not been fully mapped.

If the 65 % reduction in reasoning steps holds across deployments, developers can slash inference latency and token‑processing costs by swapping in the publicly released LoRA adapters for the Qwen3 models (provided in the think‑leakage repository) that implement the reward‑shaping objective, without retraining the base model. This cheap post‑hoc tweak turns expensive chain‑of‑thought pipelines into leaner, faster decision engines.

🦥 LazyFlow AI — Do Less, Breathe More

What if productivity wasn't about doing more, but about making everyday tasks easier?

This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 3: Slow and Steady.

💡 What I Built

Meet LazyFlow AI, a lightweight productivity assistant designed for people who want to get things done without making their day unnecessarily complicated.

We all have those days when our to-do lists feel endless, assignments seem overwhelming, and even deciding where to start takes too much energy.

LazyFlow AI is built around one simple idea: make the first step easier.

📝 Smart To-Do Planner: Add tasks, track your progress, and keep your responsibilities organized.

⚡ Lazy Mode: Break overwhelming tasks into smaller, more manageable steps.

📄 Quick Summarizer: Turn long text into a shorter version so you can review information more easily.

🌙 Wind-Down Planner: Get a gentle evening routine based on how you're feeling.

🤖 Local AI Integration: Connect an open-weight AI model through Ollama to generate personalized task breakdowns, summaries, and routines.

The goal isn't to avoid work. It's to reduce the unnecessary effort involved in organizing it.

🚀 Demo

🌐 Live Website: https://anshikasingh139.github.io/LazyFlow-AI/

Explore the dashboard, try the productivity tools, and see how LazyFlow makes everyday planning simpler.

The basic tools work directly in the browser. The generative AI features require a compatible local model and a working Ollama connection.

💻 Code

🔗 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/AnshikaSingh139/LazyFlow-AI

The project is built with three core files:

  • index.html — Website structure and dashboard.
  • style.css — Responsive layout, styling, and animations.
  • script.js — Task management, productivity tools, fallback logic, and optional local AI integration.

I kept the frontend lightweight so that the project is easy to understand, modify, and extend.

🛠️ How I Built It

I used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build the website, with a nature-inspired interface and a minimal, calming design.

For the AI component, I designed an optional integration with Ollama and Gemma 3 1B, allowing a compatible model to run locally instead of requiring every request to go through a hosted AI API.

Here's how the application works:

  1. A user enters a task, some text, or their current mood.
  2. JavaScript prepares a prompt for the relevant tool.
  3. If Ollama is available and configured correctly, the application sends the prompt to the local model.
  4. The model generates a response, which is displayed in the interface.
  5. If local AI is unavailable, the application falls back to simpler browser-based functionality.

The fallback features are intentionally basic. For example, the summarizer uses sentence selection rather than generative AI when a model isn't available.

This approach allowed me to build a usable prototype without making a hosted AI service mandatory.

One important detail: The deployed GitHub Pages version is a static website. Local AI requests run on the user's own computer only when the local model is installed, running, and accessible to the browser.

🌍 Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For me, open innovation is about having more control over the technology we build with.

Using an open-weight model creates opportunities to experiment with local inference, customize prompts, and explore different models without depending entirely on a proprietary AI API.

Here's why that matters for LazyFlow AI:

🔐 Privacy and control: When prompts are processed by a properly configured local model, they can stay on the user's machine instead of being sent to a hosted AI provider.

💸 Less dependence on paid APIs: The project doesn't require a paid AI API key for its basic features or its optional local-model integration.

🔧 Freedom to experiment: Developers can change prompts, try compatible models, and adapt the application to different productivity needs.

💻 Local-first possibilities: Running AI locally opens the door to more private, customizable applications and, with additional offline support, experiences that depend less on an internet connection.

Of course, local AI still uses computing resources, and the current website loads Google Fonts externally. The project isn't completely offline yet.

I wanted to explore how open-weight AI could make a small, practical tool more flexible without making the technology unnecessarily complicated.

🦥 The Lazy Payoff

Imagine opening your to-do list and seeing five tasks that all feel equally urgent.

Instead of spending extra time figuring out where to begin, LazyFlow can help turn one task into a series of smaller actions.

That is the payoff I'm aiming for: less time organizing the work, less friction getting started, and more freedom to work at your own pace.

The project is still an early prototype, so I don't have verified time-saving measurements yet. I'd love to improve it further by adding smarter task prioritization, a low-energy mode, and better offline support.

🏆 Prize Categories

Project focus:

  • Open-Weight AI
  • Local AI / Local Inference
  • Productivity Automation

I'll align these with the challenge's official partner categories where applicable.

🌱 What's Next?

I'd like to explore:

  • A dedicated Low-Energy Mode that prioritizes one manageable task.
  • Better AI-generated summaries.
  • A focus timer with flexible breaks.
  • Improved offline support.
  • More options for selecting locally installed models.

LazyFlow AI started with a simple thought: productivity tools don't always need to push us to do more. Sometimes, they should help us make things easier.

You relax. LazyFlow handles the busywork. 🦥🌿

Thanks for checking out my project!

items.title: OpenCode Console breach exposes API keys of 1.4% of users
items.summary: OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent, said on Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight. The company wrote on X that the breach affected 1.4% of users of OpenCode Console, its online platform, where some users keep the API keys they use to reach AI services. It emailed everyone affected that morning, and says users who received no email were not impacted. What was exposed The exposed keys were limited to Console workspaces. Co-founder Dax Raad said the open source app and the command-line tool were not affected, and that keys used there never reach OpenCode. Developers reported spend alerts from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google firing overnight. Some reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on a single account, and a few reported totals above $1,000. Anthropic and Google blocked the keys they believed were exposed. OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and would refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode says refunds for unauthorized charges are underway. What is still unclear OpenCode described the incident as tied to a large-scale distillation attack. It did not explain how that worked. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch and said it was a plain breach, with use for distillation unproven. The company has also not said how attackers got into the older system, how the keys were stored, or how far the misuse went. It describes the incident as ongoing. Affected users have been told to revoke their keys and replace them directly with each provider. The defence problem Raad said attackers had been trying to get into OpenCode's systems nonstop for 48 hours, so the team kept AI defensive agents running around the clock. The AI models it used to analyse the attack helped for a while, then began refusing when the malicious code tripped their safety filters. OpenCode later got access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users models less likely to refuse defensive security work. Raad said that improved the team's ability to investigate. The source notes that Hugging Face reported something similar in July, when commercial models blocked it from analysing logs from an intrusion. What to do now Find out whether your team used OpenCode Console and whether anyone received the notification email. Revoke and replace any key that was stored there, at each provider. Check provider billing for unexpected usage and turn on spend alerts where they are not set. Inventory where other provider keys are stored in third-party hosted tools.
