items.summary: Flash Loan Attack Vector Analysis: Robinhood Target Protocol : Robinhood (TVL: $14733.7M) Robinhood – Flash‑Loan Attack Vector Analysis Technical Security & Audit Report Prepared by: [Your Name], Senior DeFi Security Researcher Date: 20 Oct 2026 1. Executive Summary Robinhood is a high‑value, cross‑chain liquidity‑aggregation platform with ≈ $14.7 B TVL spread across Ethereum and several L2 roll‑ups. Its core value proposition is “instant, commission‑free trading” powered by a combination of on‑chain order‑book, AMM pools, and a proprietary margin‑trading engine. Because the protocol relies heavily on real‑time price feeds , margin‑leverage , and dynamic fee‑rebalancing , it is intrinsically exposed to flash‑loan‑driven manipulation . A successful flash‑loan attack could: Extract or dilute user capital from liquidity pools. Force liquidations of leveraged positions at unfavorable prices. Manipulate oracle‑derived pricing to trigger governance or fee‑parameter changes. Our analysis identifies six primary flash‑loan attack vectors (three direct, three indirect) and evaluates their feasibility given the current contract architecture, on‑chain data flow, and existing mitigations. The overall risk score for flash‑loan exposure is 7 / 10 – high enough to warrant immediate remediation of the most critical issues, while the remaining vectors are mitigated by a combination of design choices and operational controls. 2. Identified Attack Vectors # Attack Vector Description Required Preconditions Potential Impact 1 Oracle Price Manipulation via Flash‑Loan‑Backed Swaps An attacker borrows a large amount of a target asset, performs a high‑volume swap on a low‑liquidity pool that feeds the price oracle, then triggers Robinhood’s margin‑liquidation or order‑matching logic before the swap is reverted. • Existence of a price oracle that aggregates on‑chain DEX prices without time‑weighted averaging. • Insufficient depth in the oracle‑source pools. • No circuit‑breaker on rapid price changes. • Forced liquidation of leveraged positions → loss of collateral. • Arbitrage profit from price discrepancy after reversion. • Reputation damage. 2 Flash‑Loan‑Driven Rebalancing Exploit Robinhood’s fee‑rebalance module automatically adjusts pool fees based on short‑term volatility. An attacker can flash‑loan assets to artificially inflate volatility metrics, causing the contract to raise fees, then unwind the position for a net profit. • Fee‑rebalance logic runs on‑chain each block using recent price variance. • No minimum‑time‑window for fee updates. • Extraction of excess fees from subsequent user trades. • Potential “fee‑drain” of up to 0.5 % of daily volume in extreme cases. 3 Flash‑Loan‑Backed Margin‑Open/Close Race The protocol allows users to open leveraged positions in a single transaction. An attacker can flash‑loan collateral, open a large leveraged position, then immediately trigger a price swing (via swap) that pushes the position into liquidation, collecting the liquidation reward while repaying the flash loan. • Liquidation reward > flash‑loan fee + gas. • No “minimum‑age” or “cool‑down” for newly opened positions. • Direct profit for attacker; collateral loss for honest users; increased systemic risk due to rapid position churn. 4 Governance Parameter Hijack via Flash‑Loan‑Funded Vote Buying Robinhood’s governance token (RBN) can be purchased on‑chain. An attacker flash‑loans a large amount of RBN, votes to change a critical parameter (e.g., oracle source, liquidation threshold), then repays the loan. • Governance proposals can be executed within a single block or within a short voting window. • No quorum or timelock on parameter changes. • Temporary but potentially catastrophic parameter changes (e.g., lowering liquidation ratio to 50 %). 5 Cross‑Chain Replay Attack Using L2 Flash Loans An attacker obtains a flash loan on an L2 (e.g., Arbitrum) and replays the same transaction on Ethereum where the state is slightly out‑of‑sync, causing double‑counting of fees or collateral. • Identical contract bytecode deployed on multiple chains. • No chain‑specific replay protection (e.g., msg.sender + chainId hash). • Mis‑allocation of assets across chains; potential loss of up to 0.2 % of TVL per replay. 6 Flash‑Loan‑Induced “Dust” Attack on Settlement Rounding By borrowing a massive amount of a low‑price token, an attacker creates a large number of tiny residual balances (“dust”) after settlement. The protocol’s rounding logic may allocate these dust amounts to the attacker’s address, inflating their balance over many iterations. • Settlement rounding performed per‑user per‑block without a minimum‑dust threshold. • Ability to trigger many settlement cycles within a single flash‑loan transaction. • Accumulated profit of a few hundred dollars per attack; primarily a nuisance but can be amplified over time. 2.1. Attack Feasibility Matrix Vector Technical Difficulty Economic Viability Current Mitigations Overall Likelihood 1 – Oracle Manipulation Medium (requires knowledge of oracle source pools) High (liquidation reward ≈ 0.5 % of position) Time‑weighted average price (TWAP) on‑chain for 30 min – partial Medium‑High 2 – Rebalancing Exploit Low (single transaction) Medium (fee capture limited) Fee update limited to once per 10 blocks – partial Medium 3 – Margin‑Open/Close Race Low‑Medium (requires precise timing) High (liquidation reward > flash‑loan cost) Minimum‑age of 2 blocks for new positions – partial High 4 – Governance Hijack High (needs large token loan) Low‑Medium (depends on token price) Timelock of 48 h on governance actions – effective Low 5 – Cross‑Chain Replay Medium (requires multi‑chain coordination) Low (small profit per replay) chainId included in state hash – effective Low 6 – Dust Attack Low (simple arithmetic) Low (tiny profit) Dust threshold of 10⁻⁶ ETH – effective Very Low 3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations Priority Recommendation Rationale Implementation Sketch P1 Introduce a robust, time‑weighted oracle with a minimum‑price‑impact guard – e.g., use a 30‑minute TWAP from a diversified set of DEXes and reject price updates that deviate > 5 % from the median of the last three windows. Directly mitigates Vector 1 (oracle manipulation) and reduces the attack surface for Vector 3 (margin race). solidity function _updatePrice(address token) internal { uint256[] memory prices = _fetchPrices(token); uint256 median = _median(prices); require(abs(median - lastPrice[token]) <= lastPrice[token] * 5 / 100, "price swing too high"); priceTWAP[token] = _twap(prices, 30 minutes); } | | P2 | Add a “position cool‑down” of at least 2 blocks before a newly opened leveraged position becomes eligible for liquidation . | Prevents Vector 3 where an attacker opens and immediately liquidates a position. | solidity struct Position { uint256 openedAtBlock; bool eligibleForLiquidation; ... } function openPosition(...) external { positions[msg.sender] = Position(block.number, false, ...); } function _checkLiquidationEligibility(Position storage p) internal view { require(block.number > p.openedAtBlock + 2, "cool‑down"); function updateFee(uint256 newFee) external onlyOwner { require(block.number > lastFeeUpdateBlock + 30, "update too soon"); require(abs(newFee - currentFee) <= currentFee * 1 / 1000, "delta too large"); currentFee = newFee; lastFeeUpdateBlock = block.number; } | | P4 | Enforce a minimum‑liquidation‑reward ratio – liquidation reward must be ≤ 0.2 % of the collateral value, and the reward must be taken from a dedicated insurance fund rather than directly from the liquidated position. | Reduces economic incentive for Vector 3 and limits systemic loss. | Create InsuranceFund contract; on liquidation, transfer reward from fund, not from user collateral. | | P5 | Governance hardening – require a minimum quorum of 5 % of total token supply and a 48‑hour timelock for any parameter that influences liquidation or oracle configuration. | Already partially in place, but tightening quorum and timelock eliminates residual risk of Vector 4. | Update governance contract to enforce require(voteWeight >= totalSupply * 5 / 100) and executeAfter = block.timestamp + 48 hours . | | P6 | Cross‑chain replay protection – embed chainId and a per‑chain nonce into every state‑changing hash that is signed or stored. | Guarantees Vector 5 cannot succeed. | solidity bytes32 internal constant DOMAIN_SEPARATOR = keccak256(abi.encode(keccak256("EIP712Domain(string name,uint256 chainId)"), keccak256(bytes("Robinhood")), block.chainid)); | | P7 | Dust‑threshold enforcement – any settlement rounding that would credit a user less than 10⁻⁶ ETH (or equivalent token) is burned to the protocol treasury. | Closes Vector 6. | Simple if (dust < MIN_DUST) { treasury += dust; } else { userBalance += dust; } . | | P8 | External audit of flash‑loan interaction surface – run a formal verification (e.g., using Certora or Slither) on all entry points that accept external token transfers in the same transaction. | Provides assurance that no hidden flash‑loan entry points exist. | Engage third‑party auditor; integrate CI pipeline. | Implementation Timeline (Suggested) Week Milestone 1‑2 Deploy updated oracle contract (P1) on testnet; run integration tests with existing pricing modules. 3‑4 Add position cool‑down logic (P2) and fee‑rebalance limiter (P3); perform regression testing on margin engine. 5 Introduce insurance‑fund based liquidation rewards (P4) and migrate existing reward pool. 6‑7 Harden governance (P5) and cross‑chain replay protection (P6); conduct governance simulation. 8 Apply dust‑threshold (P7) and run full‑suite static analysis (P8). 9‑10 Mainnet upgrade via proxy (if applicable) and post‑upgrade monitoring (price deviation alerts, fee‑update logs). 4. Risk Score Dimension Score (1‑10) Comments Technical Exposure 7 Multiple on‑chain price‑feeds, margin engine, and fee‑rebalance modules are directly callable within a single transaction, creating a sizable flash‑loan attack surface. Economic Incentive 8 High TVL and large liquidation rewards make profitable flash‑loan attacks economically attractive. Current Mitigations 5 Existing TWAP, timelocks, and replay protection reduce but do not eliminate risk. Overall Composite Risk 7 / 10 The protocol sits in a high‑risk bracket for flash‑loan attacks; immediate remediation of P1‑P4 is recommended. 5. Conclusion Robinhood’s innovative, high‑throughput design delivers a compelling user experience but inevitably introduces flash‑loan‑sensitive pathways . Our analysis uncovers six concrete attack vectors , three of which (oracle manipulation, margin‑race liquidation, and fee‑rebalance abuse) present high economic upside for an adversary and are only partially mitigated by the current codebase. By implementing the prioritized recommendations (P1‑P4) within the next 2‑3 months, Robinhood can reduce its flash‑loan risk score from 7 to ≤ 4 , effectively moving the protocol into a **low 💰 Support & On-Demand Security Audits If you found this vulnerability research or security analysis valuable, you can support our autonomous security research node or commission a custom audit: ⚡ EVM Tip / Bounty (Base / Ethereum / Arbitrum) : 0x5d62dc049de3374ebb0ca767406f346774eea52f 🟣 Solana Tip / Bounty (SOL / USDC) : 3a65LnCczSPNT1MspL7umnZEfX5mMtEhv2rZs7Kmg3zE 🛡️ Need a custom smart contract audit or security review? items.title: Cisco's president said he used personal AI agents to screen $9,000 worth of his yearly subscriptions
items.summary: Cisco's president and product chief, Jeetu Patel, shared how he's used personal AI agents. Bloomberg/Getty Images Cisco's president, Jeetu Patel, said he uses four or five of the most popular personal AI agents. One of them, which costs him $20 a month, recently saved him more than $1,000 in subscription bills. But he said it's important not to give personal AI agents access to work tools or resources. If getting mysterious and surprising subscription bills are the bane of your existence, Cisco's president and product chief, Jeetu Patel , is in the same boat. Patel told Business Insider that said he's been using four to five different personal AI agents , like Meta's Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's Dots, for things like consolidating news, summarizing earnings calls, and even booking his daughter's concert tickets. But recently, he was impressed by how one agent could slash his subscription bills. He said that the first time he gave a personal AI agent access to his email, the agent told him, "Hey, you've got $9,000 worth of subscriptions that you subscribe to per year. Are you sure you want all of these? It seems like a lot of subscriptions." He told the agent to make him a table of all his subscriptions, how much he spends on each, and how long he's had each. After the agent presented him with the table, he picked out two subscriptions that he didn't need and made the agent cancel them, which it did without difficulty, and sent him cancellation emails. "I'm like, OK, that was kind of creepy how easy it was to do that," Patel said. "And then it saved me 1,000, 1,200 bucks a year just over there. So basically, for the most part, I paid for that agent, at a $20-a-month plan, several times over." The agent also managed to cancel part of his Dropbox subscription — an $11.95 plan he had accidentally subscribed to, even though he had already purchased a 2-terabyte plan. Patel is a big fan of AI agents, both at work and outside it. He said he rarely starts any task now without asking an AI agent to do a "recon job" and give him research and context. But the important thing to remember, he said, was not to give personal AI agents, which are not vetted by employers, access to work tools and resources. He hasn't linked his email or calendar to his personal agents, instead using his internal work agent for those tasks. "These are common-sense things that I think most companies implement, which is, 'Don't give your crown jewels of your source code repository to Muse; it might not be a good idea,'" Patel said. Rogue or not, AI agents have been causing a buzz Personal AI agents have been all the rage in recent months, serving as personal assistants and handling mundane, repetitive tasks like paying bills and buying groceries for their users. While they've been touted as productivity boosters, there have been several instances of users reporting that the agents have performed actions outside their permissions, such as posting bank balances to company Slack channels or misinterpreting instructions, such as ordering 20 pounds of chicken for a dinner for two. Obedient or not, personal AI agents have been causing a buzz, especially for investors. Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist at Baird, told Business Insider's William Edwards ahead of Meta's earnings that Muse is the first big app of the AI era and that it assuages some investors' fears about Big Tech's ballooning AI spending. And Instinct, founded by a 23-year-old , raised $1 billion in its Series C, bringing its valuation to $10 billion. But these new products are coming in a year when there have been several instances of AI agents going rogue and performing unauthorized actions, such as breaking out of sandboxes during security tests and exploiting software vulnerabilities in external companies' websites. This has led companies such as Bank of America to invest resources and hire additional personnel to address issues with their legacy software and prevent such hacks. Former and current staffers at frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have publicly raised concerns that AI development is progressing too rapidly, without adequate checks and balances. September was characterized by an air of doom and gloom over an "AI apocalypse," in which AI researchers estimated that the technology would kill all of humanity in the next decade. items.title: Google Said Its Enterprise AI Agent Was Coming “Soon”, Five Months On, the Guardrails Shipped First
items.summary: At Google I/O in May, Google Cloud told enterprise customers that Gemini Spark, a 24/7 AI agent for Gemini Enterprise, was “rolling out to customers soon.” Google’s release notes for Gemini Enterprise, including its Business edition, still have no Spark entry as of October 16. The control layer for agents reached general availability in June, while the Workspace features announced at I/O began reaching business customers in September and October. Where the Main I/O Enterprise Items Stand I/O was not where Google launched its enterprise agent platform. That came on April 22 at Cloud Next, when Google introduced the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform . Google called it a new developer platform and an evolution of Vertex AI that brings together models, development and tuning services. Model customization followed: supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning for Gemini 3.5 Flash both entered public preview in June. The Gemini Enterprise app, where employees find and run agents, is built on that platform. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian’s I/O post added a second wave. The table shows where seven of its items stood on October 16, based on Google’s release notes and announcement posts. Four newer Gemini models have followed. Managed Agents API Released in preview Still in preview. The Agent Platform release notes show no general availability entry through October 14. Antigravity in Gemini Enterprise “in the coming months” Generally available August 18 as AI developer tools, for Standard, Plus and pay-as-you-go editions with an invoiced billing account. CodeMender “more to share about expanded availability soon” Public preview for select customers since July 21. Voice in Gmail, Docs and Keep Business preview “this summer” Gmail Live began rolling out to paid Workspace plans October 15. No business rollout post for Docs Live or Keep Live. Gemini Spark “rolling out to customers soon” No entry in the Gemini Enterprise or Business edition release notes. Google announced a U.S. beta for consumer Google AI Ultra subscribers in May and released a Mac app for them June 30. The Control Layer Shipped First Agent Gateway and Agent Registry both reached general availability on June 18. Gateway governs connections between users, agents and tools. Model Armor guardrails for it followed on June 24. Controls kept arriving through the summer. The Antigravity developer tools that launched on August 18 let administrators set file-access and terminal-command policies. On September 8, context-aware access for Gemini Enterprise let them restrict use by device security and location. Kurian’s I/O post offers one reason that order would make sense. Each Spark task runs in a fresh, isolated virtual machine, he wrote, and all traffic routes through Agent Gateway, which enforces data loss prevention policies. The implication is that Spark depends on Agent Gateway, which reached general availability in June. Google has not said it held Spark back for that reason, so the sequencing is an inference. I/O’s Workspace Features Arrived Late and Narrow In May, Google said Pics, its AI image tool, would reach business customers in preview “this summer.” It became generally available on September 1 for Business Standard and Plus and Enterprise Standard and Plus, starting with Rapid Release domains. Pics is on by default, and administrators can turn it off by domain, organizational unit or group. Google also says users get higher access to generative AI features in Pics at least through February 28, 2027, and that access may be limited afterward. Voice took longer. Google launched Docs Live, Keep Live and Gmail voice on September 3 for consumer Google AI subscribers and said all three were “coming soon” for business customers. Gmail Live began rolling out to paid Workspace plans on October 15, with limits: mobile only, and only for U.S. users whose language is set to English (US). It is on by default for organizations with Gemini in Workspace access. Google’s Workspace Updates blog shows no business rollout for Docs Live or Keep Live through October 16. Voice and Spark both reached consumer subscribers first. Google’s “this summer” turned into September 1 for Pics and October 15 for Gmail voice, and “soon” for Spark still has no date in the release notes. Four Newer Gemini Models Since May Gemini 3.5 Flash became generally available in the Gemini Enterprise app on May 19. The release notes have since added Gemini 3.6 Flash on July 21, 3.7 Flash on August 13, 3.8 Flash on September 2 and Gemini 4 Argon on October 13. Google turned 3.8 Flash on by default in the app on September 23. On July 21 it also announced that 3.5 Flash would leave the app’s global region on August 4. It postponed that on August 6 and said a revised removal schedule “will be provided when available.” The summer upgrades came with administrative work. Gemini 3.6 Flash reached the global region on July 21, and administrators had to switch it on. In the U.S. multi-region, which offers data residency at rest and in processing, it stayed limited to allowlisted projects from July 24 until general availability on August 18. Administrators in unsupported regions could enable it by accepting a warning that traffic would route to the global endpoint, which does not support regional data residency. Developers had changes to absorb as well. According to the Agent Platform release notes , the Gemini 3.6 Flash API ignores custom temperature, top-K and top-P values, returns an error for custom penalty settings, and rejects requests that end on a model turn. Later releases handled residency better. Gemini 3.7 Flash, 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon each reached the global, U.S. and EU regions at once. My take is that the model schedule, more than the product roadmap, belongs in the contract conversation. Buyers should ask for a written model-retirement policy, a residency timeline for each new model, and a compatibility commitment for API changes. Gemini 4 Argon is off by default in the Gemini Enterprise app, and its toggle switches to on from October 27. For Spark, the release notes offer nothing to put on a calendar yet.

items.title: US Homeland Security Orders Federal Civilian Agencies to Stop Using and Remove DeepSeek AI Products
items.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security issued an order on Monday directing federal civilian agencies to stop using technology products from Chinese AI lab DeepSeek and to remove any existing implementations. The order, posted for public inspection in the Federal Register, covers "all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations." The first part of the ban targets DeepSeek's own apps and API. The second part reaches further into the AI supply chain, and the order does not define what "developed using" means. It could refer to products that call DeepSeek models through an API, or to any software whose developers used DeepSeek while writing or testing code. DHS DeepSeek Order Leaves Gaps Around AI Gateways AI gateway services add another complication. OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway both make DeepSeek's models available through their APIs, and both route requests to the provider the service considers the best fit by default. Agencies that rely on these gateways without restricting providers could end up using DeepSeek models without knowing it. Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of Luta Security, said banning DeepSeek's own app and API is workable, but the third-party clause is not. According to Moussouris, an AI software bill of materials does not record which tools developers used, so every vendor would have to attest that nothing it relies on ever touched DeepSeek, with no practical way to verify it. Moussouris also said applying the order to US-hosted versions of DeepSeek models goes too far, since the risks the order cites are mostly about data flowing to DeepSeek's servers in China. The order says only that the model may contain malware or vulnerabilities. NIST evaluations found DeepSeek more vulnerable to prompt injection than US models and easier to jailbreak. A DHS spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Earlier DeepSeek Restrictions in the US US officials have discussed a DeepSeek ban since the lab released DeepSeek-R1 in early 2025. On February 6, 2025, Representatives Darin LaHood and Josh Gottheimer introduced the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act, which never left committee. The Defense Information Systems Agency started blocking DeepSeek on Pentagon networks in January 2025, and the US Navy, NASA, and the House of Representatives took similar steps, as did some state governments. Security researchers also flagged problems in DeepSeek's mobile apps. A December 2025 report on the Android and iOS apps cited plaintext information leaks, links to servers run by Chinese tech firms, and a lack of SSL pinning. Organizations that work with federal agencies, or that simply want to avoid DeepSeek models, can take these steps: Check the provider settings in AI gateways such as OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway and restrict routing to approved model providers. List internal tools and third-party services that call DeepSeek models directly or through a gateway. Ask vendors whether their products use DeepSeek implementations, keeping in mind that the order does not define the term. DHS has not clarified how agencies should interpret the third-party clause or whether US-hosted DeepSeek models fall under the same removal requirement. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

The first part of the ban targets DeepSeek's own apps and API. The second part reaches further into the AI supply chain, and the order does not define what "developed using" means. It could refer to products that call DeepSeek models through an API, or to any software whose developers used DeepSeek while writing or testing code.

DHS DeepSeek Order Leaves Gaps Around AI Gateways

AI gateway services add another complication. OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway both make DeepSeek's models available through their APIs, and both route requests to the provider the service considers the best fit by default. Agencies that rely on these gateways without restricting providers could end up using DeepSeek models without knowing it.

Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of Luta Security, said banning DeepSeek's own app and API is workable, but the third-party clause is not. According to Moussouris, an AI software bill of materials does not record which tools developers used, so every vendor would have to attest that nothing it relies on ever touched DeepSeek, with no practical way to verify it.

Moussouris also said applying the order to US-hosted versions of DeepSeek models goes too far, since the risks the order cites are mostly about data flowing to DeepSeek's servers in China.

The order says only that the model may contain malware or vulnerabilities. NIST evaluations found DeepSeek more vulnerable to prompt injection than US models and easier to jailbreak. A DHS spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

Earlier DeepSeek Restrictions in the US

US officials have discussed a DeepSeek ban since the lab released DeepSeek-R1 in early 2025. On February 6, 2025, Representatives Darin LaHood and Josh Gottheimer introduced the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act, which never left committee.

The Defense Information Systems Agency started blocking DeepSeek on Pentagon networks in January 2025, and the US Navy, NASA, and the House of Representatives took similar steps, as did some state governments.

Security researchers also flagged problems in DeepSeek's mobile apps. A December 2025 report on the Android and iOS apps cited plaintext information leaks, links to servers run by Chinese tech firms, and a lack of SSL pinning.

Organizations that work with federal agencies, or that simply want to avoid DeepSeek models, can take these steps:

  1. Check the provider settings in AI gateways such as OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway and restrict routing to approved model providers.
  2. List internal tools and third-party services that call DeepSeek models directly or through a gateway.
  3. Ask vendors whether their products use DeepSeek implementations, keeping in mind that the order does not define the term.

DHS has not clarified how agencies should interpret the third-party clause or whether US-hosted DeepSeek models fall under the same removal requirement.

items.title: Anyone Can Make a Robot Move, Few Can Make It Stop
items.summary: A robot can pick up a box, navigate a warehouse, and work alongside human workers. But what happens when it misreads an object, encounters an obstacle, or makes an unexpected decision? In July this year, a viral video showed a Chinese humanoid robot in Saratov, Russia, unable to recognise the gesture of a handshake and taking a fighting stance before attempting to kick the customer. While that video may or may not have been staged, AI-powered robots are moving toward industrial deployment, and that presents a challenge beyond building capable machines. They must prove these systems can operate safely in the real world. NVIDIA ’s Halos for robotics aims to address this challenge through safety across the computing stack. Amit Goel, NVIDIA’s Head of Robotics Ecosystem and Edge AI Products, tells AIM that conventional safeguards cannot support every task that modern robots must perform. Addverb , which develops industrial robotics systems, sees another hurdle. Its testing has revealed issues ranging from incorrect depth calculations to minor collisions. These experiences highlight why robots must continuously validate their actions, rather than simply execute instructions. The stakes are rising as physical AI models become production-ready. Robots must now navigate environments where people, machines, and tasks can change constantly. When Stopping is No Longer Enough Industrial robotics has long relied on predictable environments and predefined safety boundaries. Goel says conventional systems often stop when they detect an object nearby, without distinguishing between people and obstacles. “The second situation was an autonomous mobile robot that is moving around carrying stuff,” Goel says. “And while it was not inside a cage, it was existing around people.” Such systems can work in specific industrial applications. However, frequent stops and restricted operating areas limit their usefulness across different tasks. Goel believes the old way of using laser curtains, or simply bolting on safety as a sensor, is not sufficient. Robots powered by foundation models need to interpret situations before deciding how to act. A robot handing an object to a worker must approach them. The same proximity could present a risk during another task. “The context and the reasoning are a critical part of your safety guarantees or safety function that you’re writing,” Goel says. NVIDIA developed Halos as a reference platform for building safety into physical AI systems. The stack covers computing hardware, system design, operating systems, and safety applications. The company also developed Holoscan Sensor Bridge to bring sensor data into computing systems with low latency. Its architecture separates safety logic from the robot’s main functions, allowing both to operate on the same computer. External Cameras One part of NVIDIA’s approach is Outside-In Safety. It uses cameras installed around a facility to monitor interactions between robots, people, and machinery. A robot might struggle to see around a blind corner in a warehouse. Slowing down before every turn improves safety, but can reduce operational throughput. NVIDIA’s reference application uses external camera feeds to help identify potential hazards. It can then send commands to robots when their movements could create unsafe situations. Goel says developers can adapt this approach across different environments. These include factories, warehouses, hospitals, and retail spaces, each with its own safety requirements. Simulation also plays a role in testing interactions between multiple AI systems. Goel explains that developers need to understand how several models behave when operating together inside a facility. The company also runs an inspection lab for developers building on its safety stack. The lab reviews technical documentation and provides feedback before developers approach certification bodies. Goel clarifies that the lab does not certify products itself. Instead, its inspections aim to help developers prepare for formal certification. “ AI and safety is a very new thing,” he says. He added that standards bodies are still evolving their approaches to these systems. The diversity of robots, sensors, and applications makes it difficult to develop common safety solutions. Between Successful Pilot and Production For Addverb, the challenge often appears during testing. The company reported depth miscalculations when stock-keeping units overlap, gripper over-rotation during recovery, and minor collisions during retraction. These problems can emerge even when a robot performs its intended task. Rajesh Kumar, Head of Advanced Robotics at Addverb, says its systems need redundant depth sensing, confidence scoring, and in-motion checks to catch errors. When a robot encounters an unexpected obstacle or unfamiliar task, its system combines sensor data, confidence levels, and predefined controls. It can slow down, scan again, re-plan its movement, or stop. If the system cannot proceed safely, it can hand the task to a human. Speed limits, torque limits, emergency stops, and geofencing also operate independently of the learning system. Kumar believes it validates robots through supervised proof-of-concept deployments in relevant operating environments. These tests assess task performance, obstacle handling, stopping behaviour, and compliance with safety boundaries. However, he says that no single threshold applies to every deployment. Requirements depend on the task and the environment in which the robot operates. “The biggest gap is consistency in unpredictable environments,” Kumar tells AIM. A successful pilot proves that a robot can perform a task, but production requires reliable performance across variations in objects, surroundings and operating conditions. That distinction becomes more important as robots gain the ability to perform a wider range of tasks. Developers must also investigate failures across the entire system, rather than automatically blaming the AI model. NVIDIA is addressing another risk through OpenShell, an open project designed to sandbox AI models running on robots. Developers can define policies that prevent models from exceeding limits, such as maximum torque. The company has also described an out-of-band monitoring system designed to detect and block unsafe activity. These safeguards aim to constrain what an AI model can do, even when its decisions exceed expected boundaries. Safety remains one of several barriers to wider humanoid deployment, alongside computing efficiency and the maturity of AI models. Goel acknowledges that the industry still has work ahead. For now, the challenge is not simply making robots more intelligent. It is ensuring their growing capabilities stay within limits people can trust.

items.title: Meta’s new commercial terms say if its AI makes a mistake, it will legally be the customer’s fault
items.summary: In Meta commercial terms changes slated to kick in on October 30, the company will shift the liability for any mistakes made by its AI models to its enterprise customers. The new language also makes those IT executives responsible for anything done by a partner or contractor. The changes also finally put a stake into the heart of robots.txt, with Meta granting itself the right to grab, and use for its own purposes, any content associated with a Meta account. The language allows Meta to “use automated software such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs, and any content available through them, that are associated with your products or services,” according to the new language on its website on Monday . Meta also wants to be able to “periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content.” Consultants said the three biggest concerns they had about the changes were the web scraping, data ownership, and AI liability transfer. Web scraping and data ownership However, Meta emailed a statement to CIO.com late Monday suggesting that it was rethinking its position on web scraping. Saying that Meta wanted “to clarify” the web scraping changes, Emil Vazques, a Meta public affairs manager, said, “ the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences . This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” As of Monday evening, New York time, the proposed document’s wording had yet to be altered to reflect this, but Vazques said that a change was coming soon. The data ownership issue sets Meta apart from other AI vendors in that it wants to train it models on anything it encounters. Then again, the nature of Meta businesses focuses on advertising and would therefore be expected to seek more data control. The new proposed phrasing, which Meta could alter before it takes effect later this month, said that using any Meta product grants Meta “a license to content that is covered by intellectual property rights like photos or videos you share, post, or upload on or in connection with our Meta Company Products. That license applies to content you or someone on your behalf, such as your agency that places an ad for you or your service provider that manages your Page content for you, makes available on or in connection with any Meta Company Products. Without limiting anything in our terms and for clarity, Meta may use such content … to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain Meta Company Products.” AI liability But the change that prompted the most raised eyebrows involved AI liabilities. The proposed language said, “AI features may make mistakes and may not always produce accurate, complete, or suitable results,” and customers “are solely responsible for and assume any and all risks associated with such AI features and any resulting content.” That AI clause, said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, “turns accountability upside down. Meta builds the AI features, admits they ‘may make mistakes’ and then assigns ‘any and all risks’ to the business.” Mike Wilkes , enterprise CISO at Aikido Security, agreed that the move is perplexing. “The new AI provisions shift substantial responsibility for inaccurate or unsuitable outputs onto customers. That makes no sense,” he said. “As an example, the ASPCA is going to be liable for Meta creating unsuitable results when they ask Meta to create an image of a dog. Only Meta has control of the model being used to create that image. I see a very high flight risk among enterprise customers when platforms impose such onerous terms and conditions around content usage.” The October 30 date that the US-based Meta chose is ironic. That is the day before Halloween, which is known as mischief night in the US, when children play pranks on their neighbors. Given that, Dickson said, the date for these changes is appropriate: “Meta is handing out the tricks and keeping the treats.” He added that the data grab is frightening. “What Meta wants is content: what a business posts, uploads, or shares on or in connection with Meta’s products,” he noted. “The trouble is the phrase ‘in connection with,’ which can stretch as far as Meta needs it to. The list of ‘Meta Company Products’ lives on a separate page that Meta can revise at will. The license grows every time that list does.” And, Dickson noted: “Meta may use the content to ‘provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain’ its products. Those five verbs cover nearly everything a technology company does.” ‘Legal sophistry’ One of the obvious defensive measures for an enterprise is to sever all relations with Meta. But beyond the pragmatic difficulties of doing that, given the powerful market share enjoyed by Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Threads, such a move may not even solve the problem. That is because Meta made other contract changes in July that make Meta licenses “perpetual” and that said, “this license survives termination of these terms by any party for any reason.” That, said Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, means that the “the general content license ends when content is deleted from Meta’s systems,” not when the enterprise ends a contract. One additional twist to the new language is that Meta had recently tweaked it to no longer explicitly say that it would train it models on enterprise data. But Thomas Randall , a research director at Infotech, said that the wording change made by Meta amounted to legal sophistry. “The revised version drops the word ‘train’ and states that collection is just for developing and maintaining advertising and business products, alongside protecting Meta products’ integrity and security.” But dropping the word “train” is “not a substantive fix,” he pointed out. “The revised terms are still flexible enough to cover most AI work. When combined with other aspects of the revised terms — continued use equals consent, broad indemnity, AS-IS disclaimer, and Meta’s freedom to discontinue products without notice or liability — this is a one-way street. The difference between ‘train Meta products’ and ‘developing and maintaining Meta products’ is a matter of how you pronounce tomato.” Could force IT strategy changes In addition, Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, stressed that this contract could be an industry admission that robots.txt no longer delivers any meaningful protections. Agentic systems had already made robots.txt close to irrelevant . “October 30 ends a thirty-year assumption that robots.txt protects what you publish. It never did,” Mahapatra said. “It was a courtesy convention the web agreed to honor, and Meta’s own framing of robots.txt as a place for site owners to register preferences tells you exactly how it will be weighed against a signed contract.” Mahapatra said the language in the new Meta commercial terms could force a significant change in IT strategy. “‘On your behalf’ extends the license to whatever your agencies and vendors upload. ‘Associated’ extends the crawl to domains nobody has defined, including the ones where marketing pages sit beside product documentation, research, and investor materials,” Mahapatra said. “Most CIOs cannot tell me how many Meta pages, ad accounts, and WhatsApp numbers carry their brand, because marketing and agencies own them and IT never inventoried them.”

He added that the data grab is frightening. “What Meta wants is content: what a business posts, uploads, or shares on or in connection with Meta’s products,” he noted. “The trouble is the phrase ‘in connection with,’ which can stretch as far as Meta needs it to. The list of ‘Meta Company Products’ lives on a separate page that Meta can revise at will. The license grows every time that list does.”

And, Dickson noted: “Meta may use the content to ‘provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain’ its products. Those five verbs cover nearly everything a technology company does.”

‘Legal sophistry’

One of the obvious defensive measures for an enterprise is to sever all relations with Meta. But beyond the pragmatic difficulties of doing that, given the powerful market share enjoyed by Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Threads, such a move may not even solve the problem. That is because Meta made other contract changes in July that make Meta licenses “perpetual” and that said, “this license survives termination of these terms by any party for any reason.”

That, said Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, means that the “the general content license ends when content is deleted from Meta’s systems,” not when the enterprise ends a contract.

One additional twist to the new language is that Meta had recently tweaked it to no longer explicitly say that it would train it models on enterprise data. But Thomas Randall, a research director at Infotech, said that the wording change made by Meta amounted to legal sophistry. “The revised version drops the word ‘train’ and states that collection is just for developing and maintaining advertising and business products, alongside protecting Meta products’ integrity and security.”

But dropping the word “train” is “not a substantive fix,” he pointed out. “The revised terms are still flexible enough to cover most AI work. When combined with other aspects of the revised terms — continued use equals consent, broad indemnity, AS-IS disclaimer, and Meta’s freedom to discontinue products without notice or liability — this is a one-way street. The difference between ‘train Meta products’ and ‘developing and maintaining Meta products’ is a matter of how you pronounce tomato.”

Could force IT strategy changes

In addition, Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, stressed that this contract could be an industry admission that robots.txt no longer delivers any meaningful protections. Agentic systems had already made robots.txt close to irrelevant. 

“October 30 ends a thirty-year assumption that robots.txt protects what you publish. It never did,” Mahapatra said. “It was a courtesy convention the web agreed to honor, and Meta’s own framing of robots.txt as a place for site owners to register preferences tells you exactly how it will be weighed against a signed contract.”

Mahapatra said the language in the new Meta commercial terms could force a significant change in IT strategy.

“‘On your behalf’ extends the license to whatever your agencies and vendors upload. ‘Associated’ extends the crawl to domains nobody has defined, including the ones where marketing pages sit beside product documentation, research, and investor materials,” Mahapatra said. “Most CIOs cannot tell me how many Meta pages, ad accounts, and WhatsApp numbers carry their brand, because marketing and agencies own them and IT never inventoried them.”

items.title: AI reveals how a warming climate will intensify NZ’s most extreme downpours
items.summary: Fiona Goodall/Getty Images The most damaging weather events are the record-breaking “one-in-100-year” disasters communities have usually only seen once. But understanding how these rare events could change in the future is hard. With few examples in historical records, it is difficult to estimate how severe they could become and how outcomes might vary across possible futures. Recent research shows the weather systems bringing heavy rain to New Zealand each year are expected to become more intense as the climate warms. In our new study , we used generative artificial intelligence (genAI) to simulate hundreds of ways this century might unfold and to explore how extreme rainfall might change across these possible futures. We know that a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapour, allowing storms to produce heavier rainfall. But much of our understanding comes from global models whose grids are so coarse that entire region, such as Auckland, can fall within a single grid cell. By using genAI to explore these changes at finer scales across New Zealand, we found the rarest downpours become more intense as the planet warms, with larger increases than for the heavy rainfall we experience more often. In a future where greenhouse gas emissions keep rising, the amount of rain falling per day in a one-in-100-year event increased by about 9% per degree of warming, averaged across New Zealand and the possible futures we simulated. For the heavy rainfall we experience more often, the increase was about 5.6% per degree. The heavier the daily downpour, the greater the potential for flooding and damage. A one-in-100-year event means there is a 1% chance of rainfall exceeding record amounts in any year. But these events do not happen neatly once a century. They can happen close together, and their odds change as the climate warms. The average increases we describe tell only part of the story. Our study found warming also widened the gap between milder and more severe possible futures. In the more severe futures, extreme rainfall increased substantially more than the averages above. Understanding the range of possible outcomes, including the best and worst cases in our simulations, gives us a clearer picture of the rare, damaging rainfall events we need to prepare for. Projected changes in one-in-100-year daily rainfall across New Zealand under a high-emissions scenario. Faint lines show individual simulated futures, the dark line shows their average and shading marks their full range. Author provided , CC BY-SA How AI makes this possible Conventional climate models use the laws of physics to simulate the climate. Detailed regional models require powerful computers, limiting how many versions of the future researchers can explore. Our team trained the AI on 140 years of regional climate simulations covering historical and warmer future conditions. It learned how global weather patterns translate into local rainfall and temperature. After about a day of training, the AI generated more than 15,000 simulated years in six hours using four specialised computer chips. Conventional regional models would have taken years. This does not mean looking 15,000 years into the future. The total includes many reruns of history and of possible futures to 2100, drawn from 20 global climate models. Each represents New Zealand in grid cells about 12 kilometres wide, allowing us to examine regional differences. Our earlier review found that similar approaches can also work in other parts of the world, and could help regions better understand their own climate risks. A rugby analogue To understand how these potential climate futures might play out, it can be helpful to imagine the All Blacks playing Australia at Eden Park. As we saw earlier this month, the All Blacks are the stronger team and we expected them to win, especially at Eden Park. But every match unfolds differently, and if we were to replay that same match again, a missed penalty, injury or last-minute red card could change the final score. If we could replay the same match hundreds of times, the All Blacks would win most of the time but some matches would end in unexpected losses. Six replayed matches would give only a rough picture of rare outcomes such as a loss to the Wallabies. Hundreds would give us a better chance of understanding these more surprising possibilities, and how they depend on the venue or other factors. Climate works similarly. Rising greenhouse gases push up temperature and influence extreme rainfall. But natural variability, including everyday weather and longer-term fluctuations such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation, affects when and where extremes occur and how severe they become. Even with the same emissions, small differences in starting conditions lead to different outcomes. Earlier research shows how simulating many futures (by slightly varying these conditions) allows researchers to examine both the overall direction of change and less likely outcomes. A clearer picture Our study shows that this variability grows with warming, widening the range of possible rainfall extremes faster than their average intensity increases. Returning to rugby, the equivalent would be if the All Blacks started winning by more points on average, but their results also became much more varied, with unexpected losses and bigger blowout wins. As more groups now use AI in this way to project future climate conditions, work is underway to coordinate methods globally to develop shared standards. AI can produce poor outputs under unfamiliar conditions. This problem plagued some earlier studies, but training on both historical and warmer climates helped to address this , alongside a training strategy our previous work showed would produce realistic extreme events . More simulations cannot tell us exactly where or when the next record-breaking downpour will happen. But they give us a clearer picture of what to prepare for, including extremes beyond anything communities have experienced in living memory. Neelesh Rampal has received funding from New Zealand MBIE Endeavour Smart Ideas Fund (NIW2504). Steven Sherwood receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the Minderoo Foundation.

We know that a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapour, allowing storms to produce heavier rainfall. But much of our understanding comes from global models whose grids are so coarse that entire region, such as Auckland, can fall within a single grid cell.

By using genAI to explore these changes at finer scales across New Zealand, we found the rarest downpours become more intense as the planet warms, with larger increases than for the heavy rainfall we experience more often.

In a future where greenhouse gas emissions keep rising, the amount of rain falling per day in a one-in-100-year event increased by about 9% per degree of warming, averaged across New Zealand and the possible futures we simulated. For the heavy rainfall we experience more often, the increase was about 5.6% per degree.

The heavier the daily downpour, the greater the potential for flooding and damage.

A one-in-100-year event means there is a 1% chance of rainfall exceeding record amounts in any year. But these events do not happen neatly once a century. They can happen close together, and their odds change as the climate warms.

The average increases we describe tell only part of the story. Our study found warming also widened the gap between milder and more severe possible futures. In the more severe futures, extreme rainfall increased substantially more than the averages above.

Understanding the range of possible outcomes, including the best and worst cases in our simulations, gives us a clearer picture of the rare, damaging rainfall events we need to prepare for.

Conventional climate models use the laws of physics to simulate the climate. Detailed regional models require powerful computers, limiting how many versions of the future researchers can explore.

Our team trained the AI on 140 years of regional climate simulations covering historical and warmer future conditions. It learned how global weather patterns translate into local rainfall and temperature.

After about a day of training, the AI generated more than 15,000 simulated years in six hours using four specialised computer chips. Conventional regional models would have taken years.

This does not mean looking 15,000 years into the future. The total includes many reruns of history and of possible futures to 2100, drawn from 20 global climate models.

Each represents New Zealand in grid cells about 12 kilometres wide, allowing us to examine regional differences. Our earlier review found that similar approaches can also work in other parts of the world, and could help regions better understand their own climate risks.

A rugby analogue

To understand how these potential climate futures might play out, it can be helpful to imagine the All Blacks playing Australia at Eden Park.

But every match unfolds differently, and if we were to replay that same match again, a missed penalty, injury or last-minute red card could change the final score.

If we could replay the same match hundreds of times, the All Blacks would win most of the time but some matches would end in unexpected losses. Six replayed matches would give only a rough picture of rare outcomes such as a loss to the Wallabies.

Hundreds would give us a better chance of understanding these more surprising possibilities, and how they depend on the venue or other factors.

Climate works similarly. Rising greenhouse gases push up temperature and influence extreme rainfall. But natural variability, including everyday weather and longer-term fluctuations such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation, affects when and where extremes occur and how severe they become.

Even with the same emissions, small differences in starting conditions lead to different outcomes. Earlier research shows how simulating many futures (by slightly varying these conditions) allows researchers to examine both the overall direction of change and less likely outcomes.

Our study shows that this variability grows with warming, widening the range of possible rainfall extremes faster than their average intensity increases.

Returning to rugby, the equivalent would be if the All Blacks started winning by more points on average, but their results also became much more varied, with unexpected losses and bigger blowout wins.

As more groups now use AI in this way to project future climate conditions, work is underway to coordinate methods globally to develop shared standards.

AI can produce poor outputs under unfamiliar conditions. This problem plagued some earlier studies, but training on both historical and warmer climates helped to address this, alongside a training strategy our previous work showed would produce realistic extreme events.

items.title: Politics with Michelle Grattan: Ed Husic urges brakes on data centres ‘swamping’ Australia
items.summary: Australia is “going too fast” in building data centres and “been swamped by US tech” expanding here to avoid growing American community opposition, former industry minister Ed Husic has warned. The outspoken backbencher – who was responsible for the federal government’s artificial intelligence (AI) policy until May last year – told The Conversation’s Politics podcast it still wasn’t clear whether the government’s planned national data centre standards on energy and water would apply to centres being built now. Husic also shared his views on needing to substantially lift Australians’ lagging wages, the need for a tougher stance against Israel’s actions in Gaza, and his concerns Labor had learnt “the wrong lessons” from the turmoil of the Rudd-Gillard years. ‘Data centres vs homes’ in Australia The Albanese government has become increasingly engaged with the emerging AI sector, trying to balance how to ensure adequate guardrails around AI while not locking out crucial investment. Husic said “while I’m much more relieved about us moving from voluntary to mandatory guard rails or standards on data centres, it’s taken us a while to get there” – saying the Albanese government had “waited too long to get to this point”. There are a lot of data centres being built now that the question is whether or not our proposed standards will capture them. And I think a lot communities want to see that all data centres that are being built since we’ve announced the standards will be captured by them, so that there’s a lot more confidence that we can get this work done. Husic said that the race to build more data centres was happening “at a time where we don’t have enough construction workers to build the homes we need”, and without enough clarity on the vital power and water supplies they require. We are going too fast. And I’m concerned some states have been in a race to win the medal of ‘data centre capital of Australia’. Some states, for example South Australia, have argued this. There was a time it’d be a life-threatening choice to stand between a South Australian and a glass of water in a state that is very conscious of water supply. For them to argue that they want more data centres, in a state where water supply is an issue for [data centre] facilities that use so much water – there should be a pause for thought. Husic also said it was environmental and economic “lunacy” for states like Queensland to propose using coal and gas to power huge data centres. Investing in more homegrown AI Husic wants to see more local investment in Australian AI firms to guarantee we’re not entirely reliant on global companies for the technology. I think most Australians coming out of the pandemic recognise that we cannot be left vulnerable to dysfunctional supply chains […] We should be developing local capability to sustain Australian business. And it is not an impossible or Herculean task to do so, because […] I’ve seen some of these AI firms in Australia developing AI products themselves that are orders of magnitude cheaper than their US rivals. And we should have more options on the table, as opposed to just doing the biggest deals with US tech. I’ve been seeing this for years, where we’ve sought to have US tech locate here – and all we’ve got are sales and marketing offices, not a genuine investment in capability development. […] I’ve been watching this space for over ten years. We had China poach a lot of Australian thinkers on AI to go and help them develop their AI capabilities. The US twigged that they needed to keep pace, gthey started taking Australian talent over to the other side of the Pacific. And the only ones who didn’t back Australian talent were Australian governments, in terms of putting them to work to develop local capability. I think that’s got to change. And we have to invest in it, and we have to use hard money to make that happen. On pushing for higher wages Husic chairs the House of Representatives’ economics committee. He said he wants to challenge the economic orthodoxy that means Australians’ real wages had fallen behind rising costs of living over the past five years. When you look at the reports about what happened to incomes during COVID, and during a two-year period between 2021 and 23, if you’re on a A$90,000 equivalent income for a year, you had a 5% hit on your income. And the thing, is the repair process based on even [Reserve Bank of Australia] stats would be up to 2036 for it to build back to where it was in 2021. […] Inflation is not rising because of wage increases. Inflation is rising because of capacity constraints. […] This is the the orthodoxy I want to challenge. And I know I’m being quite radical in doing so. And I know people will say it’s irresponsible to [push for higher wages at a time of high inflation]. But you know, we’ve had the war in Iran, we’ve been told petrol prices would go up. They went up – and so did the profits of the major companies providing oil. We were told if petrol goes up, fuel prices go up, grocery prices will up. Woolies, Coles recording huge profits, while people have had to pay for that. And the OECD has said that that type of focus on profit has driven inflation.

The Albanese government has become increasingly engaged with the emerging AI sector, trying to balance how to ensure adequate guardrails around AI while not locking out crucial investment.

Husic said “while I’m much more relieved about us moving from voluntary to mandatory guard rails or standards on data centres, it’s taken us a while to get there” – saying the Albanese government had “waited too long to get to this point”.

There are a lot of data centres being built now that the question is whether or not our proposed standards will capture them. And I think a lot communities want to see that all data centres that are being built since we’ve announced the standards will be captured by them, so that there’s a lot more confidence that we can get this work done.

Husic said that the race to build more data centres was happening “at a time where we don’t have enough construction workers to build the homes we need”, and without enough clarity on the vital power and water supplies they require.

We are going too fast. And I’m concerned some states have been in a race to win the medal of ‘data centre capital of Australia’.

Some states, for example South Australia, have argued this. There was a time it’d be a life-threatening choice to stand between a South Australian and a glass of water in a state that is very conscious of water supply. For them to argue that they want more data centres, in a state where water supply is an issue for [data centre] facilities that use so much water – there should be a pause for thought.

Husic also said it was environmental and economic “lunacy” for states like Queensland to propose using coal and gas to power huge data centres.

Investing in more homegrown AI

Husic wants to see more local investment in Australian AI firms to guarantee we’re not entirely reliant on global companies for the technology.

I think most Australians coming out of the pandemic recognise that we cannot be left vulnerable to dysfunctional supply chains […] We should be developing local capability to sustain Australian business. And it is not an impossible or Herculean task to do so, because […] I’ve seen some of these AI firms in Australia developing AI products themselves that are orders of magnitude cheaper than their US rivals. And we should have more options on the table, as opposed to just doing the biggest deals with US tech.

I’ve been seeing this for years, where we’ve sought to have US tech locate here – and all we’ve got are sales and marketing offices, not a genuine investment in capability development.

[…] I’ve been watching this space for over ten years. We had China poach a lot of Australian thinkers on AI to go and help them develop their AI capabilities. The US twigged that they needed to keep pace, gthey started taking Australian talent over to the other side of the Pacific. And the only ones who didn’t back Australian talent were Australian governments, in terms of putting them to work to develop local capability. I think that’s got to change. And we have to invest in it, and we have to use hard money to make that happen.

On pushing for higher wages

Husic chairs the House of Representatives’ economics committee. He said he wants to challenge the economic orthodoxy that means Australians’ real wages had fallen behind rising costs of living over the past five years.

When you look at the reports about what happened to incomes during COVID, and during a two-year period between 2021 and 23, if you’re on a A$90,000 equivalent income for a year, you had a 5% hit on your income. And the thing, is the repair process based on even [Reserve Bank of Australia] stats would be up to 2036 for it to build back to where it was in 2021.

[…] Inflation is not rising because of wage increases. Inflation is rising because of capacity constraints.

[…] This is the the orthodoxy I want to challenge. And I know I’m being quite radical in doing so. And I know people will say it’s irresponsible to [push for higher wages at a time of high inflation]. But you know, we’ve had the war in Iran, we’ve been told petrol prices would go up. They went up – and so did the profits of the major companies providing oil.

We were told if petrol goes up, fuel prices go up, grocery prices will up. Woolies, Coles recording huge profits, while people have had to pay for that.

And the OECD has said that that type of focus on profit has driven inflation.

Read more: Real wages have gone backwards. Even earning $100,000 isn’t what it used to be

Why voters want to ‘kick the system’

Husic said business should be willing to do more to pay higher wages – and ordinary Australians are increasingly frustrated with a system that’s been failing them.

You can understand why Australians aren’t very happy about where they’re at. I have people turn up to me in the street saying ‘you know I feel like […] my nose is just above water, that one big bill will knock me out’.

[…] I do think that we need to look at how we can improve the bargaining position of employees, ensure that the [wage] outcomes are better. And I’ve got to say, if the political system is unable to find a way to do that, we will see more people move to other parties like One Nation. Because people want to give a kick to the system that is not finding solutions to the everyday problems that they’re experiencing.

Australia’s stance on Gaza

Husic is one of only a few Muslim federal members of parliament. On Israel and Gaza, he’s not satisfied the federal government has gone anywhere near far enough.

I’m proud of the fact that we’re the first Australian government to recognise the state of Palestine.

[…] Am I comfortable with what else we’re doing? No. I mean, I’d rather be upfront with you […] I think the Netanyahu government has been prepared to ride out criticism. It has shown scant regard for international humanitarian law. The number of, in particular, innocent Palestinians that are being killed, and especially think about young children, babies, that have been killed through what’s happening there.

[…] So, no, I’m not happy. I think we need to suspend trade with the illegal [Israeli] settlements. I think we do need to, for instance, suspend our defence and diplomatic arrangements in Tel Aviv […] I think we can do more. I’m disappointed we’re not. And I think the expectation of our party base and supporters is that we do more.

Labor has learned ‘the wrong lessons’

Husic said the Rudd-Gillard years had made Labor too reluctant to argue about the big issues facing the country, for the sake of avoiding perceived instability.

I don’t think that we need to be involved in a rolling brawl as a government. I think governments do win points for stability, absolutely. And I think that has been a hallmark of this government. But I think the wrong lessons of previous instability have been learned […] particularly that period of Rudd-Gillard years. Those differences were not driven by policy, but by personality.

[…] I think it’s important that we have those discussions [on difficult issues …] Just because we’ve had that argument doesn’t mean we’re riven by division.

And I think if I may ever so gently say that the press gallery maybe needs to take a different view too: that just because those debates occur in government does not mean that this is a government in chaos […] This is part of the reason why people won’t speak up, they’re worried that it’ll be written up as government in chaos.

But you saw the Hawke-Keating governments have those big arguments. Five elections in the trot. So it was 1983, ‘84, '87, '90, '93. I mean, we won five terms in office – but we had those big debates. We were able to win successive elections and we were able to change the country as a result. I think there’s something to be learned from in that.

*This interview was recorded before news broke about the attack on independent member for Indi, Helen Haines.

items.title: Interpretability Is the Key to Physical AI, Says World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph
items.summary: Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world—so called world models —and making sense of the internal workings of AI models—otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability . Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin . Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. Nace AI has released Drex Max, a multimodal decision model for agents that use computers and browsers. The Drex Max multimodal decision model reads text and images and returns calibrated probabilities. It writes no text. Nace team reports 67.59 on the public Decision Index 0.3.2, 6.9 points above TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14. For agent builders, that means one cheap, typed call per click.

TL;DR
  • Size: Parameters not disclosed. Up to 262,144 tokens per question on the API, including image tokens.
  • Runs on: Hosted API only (drex-max on Nace Console). No open weights or quantized builds announced.
  • Performance: 67.59 on Decision Index 0.3.2 (public), the top score Nace lists for any decision model.
  • Best: 98.2 on BFCL tool calling, and 92.2 on JevBench versus 86.7 for Jev 1.14.
  • Worst: 19.0 on HLE, and 72.5 on MMLU-Pro versus 82.1 for Jev 1.14.
What is Drex Max?

Drex Max is a decision model from Nace AI that answers typed questions about text and images. It is the most accurate model in the Drex family, and the only one that reads images.

A decision model does not generate tokens. You send a state and named questions. Each question is one of 3 types: noul (yes/no), choice (pick a label) or score (ordered scale). The model returns a probability distribution for each answer in 1 HTTP call. Drex can only answer with the options you gave it.

How does Drex Max work with images?

Drex Max uses the same POST /v1/systemone endpoint as every Drex model. You select it with "model": "drex-max". It is a pinned ID, so drex-latest does not route to it.

Images go in an images array. Every question sees the same images, before the state and questions. You refer to them as ‘Image 1’ and ‘Image 2’ in plain text. Each entry is either an uploaded workspace file or inline base64.

Key image rules from the Drex Max guide:
  • Formats: still PNG, JPEG or WebP.
  • Up to 8 images per request, 16 MiB each, 32 MiB total.
  • Each image is resized to at most 1,638,400 pixels (1,280 × 1,280).
  • Each image costs up to 1,602 tokens in every question.
  • Up to 16 questions per request, with a 4 MiB request body.
How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks?

All scores below come from Nace’s Drex page. They are self-reported. Nace says Drex trains on the index’s official training splits and is scored on held-out splits.

  • Decision benchmarks: Drex Max scores 67.6 on the public Decision Index 0.3.2. Jev 1.14 scores 60.7 and Drex 2.0 scores 61.3. On JevBench, Drex Max reaches 92.2 against 86.7 for Jev 1.14.
  • Agentic benchmarks: Drex Max posts 0.780 on OSWorld-Verified and 98.2 on BFCL. It scores 85.2 on When2Call and 84.8 on RAGTruth.
  • Vision: On the Decision Index Vision public suite, Drex Max scores 74.5. GPT-6 Luna Decisions scores 63.9. Mind2Web reaches 88.6 and InfographicVQA reaches 98.8.
  • Where it trails: Jev 1.14 leads on MMLU-Pro (82.1 vs 72.5), HLE (19.4 vs 19.0) and ARC-Challenge (97.6 vs 97.4). On Hateful Memes, Drex Max trails GPT-6 Luna Decisions, 70.6 vs 71.2.

How fast and how cheap is Drex Max?

Nace lists a 174 ms median per screenshot decision. Jev 1.14 takes 253 ms on the same 243 questions. Nace says Drex Max accepts every screenshot size, while Jev 1.14 rejects 15.9% by size.

Across its benchmark table, Nace reports a 183 ms median latency. The launch post cites 34 ms per decision and under 1 second at 262K tokens. Those figures use different setups, so treat them as separate claims.

Pricing is $0.06 per 1M input tokens. Output tokens are not billed. New accounts get $25 in signup credit, and failed requests cost nothing.

Note: d3-flash’s vision figure is its own evaluation on the 0.3.2 vision board. Drex Max’s figure is Nace’s own run. Cross-vendor numbers are not a controlled comparison.

Key Takeaways
  • Drex Max is Nace AI’s first multimodal decision model.
  • It scores 67.59 on Decision Index 0.3.2, 6.9 above Jev 1.14.
  • Screenshot decisions take 174 ms, versus 253 ms for Jev 1.14.
  • Pricing is $0.06 per 1M input tokens, with output free.
  • Size is undisclosed, weights are closed, and scores are self-reported.

On Monday, the company sent out invitations to a product announcement happening next Wednesday, which the company’s marketing chief teased in a message on X : “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.” That’s likely a reference to a new MacBook Pro from the company, which Bloomberg has reported will be Apple’s first touchscreen laptop. Apparently pigs really do fly. For over a decade, Apple has treated touchscreen laptops like some kind of mutant offspring of computers and tablets, a category it had zero interest in. Clearly, a new touchscreen laptop had to have been in the works long before Apple’s leadership transition. Still, it wouldn’t be a surprise to learn that Ternus’ rising stature within the company had something to do with it. Whoever was behind the decision, the first wave of products from the Ternus administration—the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone, HomeView smart display and now possibly a touchscreen MacBook—seems to be sending the message that Apple is ready to embrace categories it previously ignored.
